We prove that von Neumann algebras associated with compact regions within abelian quantum double models have infinite type $II$.

To enhance magnon-phonon entanglement in cavity magnomechanics, we introduce a new approach by simultaneously applying two modulated fields. The first field modifies the coupling between the magnons and cavity, while the second modulates the coupling between the magnons and phonons. By synchronizing the time variations of these fields, an additional entanglement-assisted force emerges, enabling the generation of stronger entangled states and facilitating access to an entanglement-assisted force regime that was previously only supported. Our theoretical findings are valid for a broad category of cavity magnomechanical systems.

We've obtained one-loop triple-collinear splitting operators for color and spin spaces, applicable to all five scenarios: $q \to qq'\bar{q}'$, $q \to qq\bar{q}$, $q \to qg\gamma$, $q \to gg\gamma$, and $q \to g\gamma$. This achievement builds on an existing framework and incorporates a novel method using the regularized angular momentum operator and operator product expansion, and also generalizes a previous formalism to the one-loop level. Verification of our result has been done through numerical and algebraic methods. This work lays the foundation for developing a parton shower algorithm that operates under a one-loop accuracy standard.

A formal power series ring General Neron Desingularization (FNRD) can be seen as a multi-variable expansion of a classical power series ring Neron Desingularization. A key aspect of FNRD involves a power series ring that has a more complex structure, specifically a local ring with a finite length. We propose an alternative version of FNRD for these types of rings, providing a more straightforward explanation and examples to support this generalization. This new formulation has the potential to be used as a tool to describe certain transformations power series rings, facilitating the study of specific algebraic structures.

The timeless motion of the celestial bodies has always held a profound impact on human life, influencing our ancestors, scholars, and religious figures, while also playing a significant role in shaping the rich history of classical Islamic civilization. The solar position's variations have been integral to constructing Islamic prayer spaces, predicting seasonal changes, and navigating through the oceans, all of which relied heavily on understanding and predicting shadow lengths. Unfortunately, the loss of historical astronomical treatises, such as those written by Muhammad ibn Yunus, has resulted in a significant gap in our current knowledge on this subject, prompting a need to utilize machine learning techniques to reconstruct the ancient solar position tracking techniques employed by Islamic astronomers. This innovative approach aims to bridge this knowledge gap, potentially providing valuable insights that could even contribute to updating the classic refraction equation in contemporary optics.

This research focuses on an integrated design of decentralized device-to-device communication and uplink link in presence of D2D interference, with a centralized decentralized cognitive radio structure. We utilize machine learning algorithms such as multi-agent reinforcement learning to achieve this objective. Specifically, we utilize machine learning techniques to solve complex optimization problems related to this integration. To effectively increase the data transmission rate in this communication system, we utilize machine learning algorithms such as regularized splitting algorithm to split the overall problem into multiple subproblems and an adaptive learning algorithm to find optimal solutions. Furthermore, to ensure the stability of these subproblems, we utilize an adaptive learning algorithm to find a suitable solution within these subproblems. Our simulation outcomes validate the effectiveness of the proposed solutions.

The surge in telework due to lockdowns has presented a unique opportunity to transfer and integrate advanced technology in the proposed research. The integration of advanced measurement techniques in various fields has led to a significant transformation in the methods of data acquisition. The proposed research involves aggregating the findings from multiple, advanced two-dimensional Laser Doppler Vibrometry and camera-based systems to enhance their respective capabilities for accurate and precise data collection. The LDV system's capabilities to capture velocity fields of samples in response to mechanical stimuli are well-documented. On the other hand, the camera-based system serves as a versatile and adaptable tool for real-time observation of simultaneous three-dimensional movements. The primary objective of this research involves leveraging the strengths of these measurement systems to develop an effective algorithm for simulating and predicting the dynamic behavior of structures under mechanical stress. The LDV and camera-based systems' data is combined to extract feature points and establish corresponding relationships, which in turn enable an estimation of structure displacements. The proposed method involves a novel approach for estimating velocity fields using the characteristics of detected features, demonstrating promising outcomes in testing the method using the fundamental vibration mode of an aluminum beam. The results indicate promising accuracy and precision levels, with an average error margin of approximately 0.003 mm, representing less than 0.003 mm error for a 10 mm estimated displacement.

The cardinalities of finite models for sentences with at least three variables, relying on one binary relationship, are examined in terms of their spectra. This study builds upon work by Alwen, who analyzed spectra with asymmetric relationships, by expanding it to cover situations where the relationship is asymmetric but also considers symmetric relationships. It is demonstrated that when accounting for both asymmetric and symmetric relationships, high-growth functions are still representable, although binary representations are no longer sufficient, as proven by an upper bound of the $(\log n)^{3/2}$ function. Additionally, it is found that when considering only sentences with relationships that are in normal form, functions represented can be shown to be in the FP hierarchy, similar to the spectra with asymmetric relationships. This study also indicates the limitation of NP-completeness for verifying model existence with symmetric relationships, as shown by a newly established hard problem, even for those relationships in normal form.

The electron beam in a Transmission Electron Microscope can be distorted by various aberrations, limiting its detective sensitivity. By applying a programmable electrostatic phase corrector, specifically a Phase Plate, one can potentially mitigate the detrimental impact of aberrations and surpass the electron energy loss spectroscopy limit of 1 eV. Our research focuses on determining the minimum delta-E resolution achievable by correcting fourth-order spherical aberration in electron beams, given a 1 eV energy loss threshold. We conducted simulations to assess the performance of Phase Plates with varying radii, ranging from 10 nm to 1000 nm, in mitigating aberrations within an energy loss spectroscopy range of 0.5 eV to 20 eV. We found that Phase Plates with sizes between 50 nm and 500 nm can effectively reduce spherical aberration, resulting in a delta-E of 1 eV, and for larger phase plates, even an aberration-free spectrum can be obtained, yielding an delta-E of 0.5 eV.

Drawing inspiration from Feynman's and Deutsch's groundbreaking work, we introduce a theoretical framework that assesses computational capability across diverse physical platforms and complexity scales. This framework is utilized to analyze the fundamental principles of quantum computation. Furthermore, this study serves as a precursor to investigating more universal computation models by examining additional physical mechanisms exemplified throughout the paper.

This study focuses on determining the general equation for calculating the potential positions of an $n$ step random walk in a $d$ dimensional space, denoted as $|S_{n, d}|$, with an emphasis on providing a proof for the case where $d$ is greater than $n$ plus one. Initially, we establish a formula that illustrates how to find $|S_{n, d}|$ when the walk's path is shorter than the space's dimensions. We then present a proof-based demonstration for the long-standing conjecture that resolved the problem when the path's length is not less than the space's dimensions.

This research investigates the influence of quantum corrections on a scalar field's behavior in an asymptotically flat Schwarzschild black hole. By utilizing the semi-classical gravity approach, modified Einstein field equations are utilized, leading to a new metric that defines a black hole with quantum properties. In an asymptotically flat space, the effect of this modification diminishes, allowing for a smooth transition. In this context, we calculate the quasinormal modes of the scalar field, analyzing their dependence on various parameters, including the mode number, frequency, and impact parameter. Our calculations demonstrate that quantum effects have a substantial impact on the behavior of quasinormal modes, with the effect's intensity decreasing as the impact parameter increases.

We have derived a semi-analytical formula for the dynamic density-density correlation of massless Dirac electrons in doped graphene, which is applicable at finite temperatures. This finding is key to understanding the thermal screening of interactions among Dirac electrons and we leverage it to calculate the thermal capacity and compressibility of doped graphene. Notably, at very low temperatures, the thermal capacity displays a linear temperature dependence characteristic of normal Fermi liquids, with the coefficient controlled by the velocity of charge carriers in the material.

Continuous speech leads to variations in tone, pitch, and rhythm, giving it its natural flow. To create high-quality, context-sensitive synthetic speech at the paragraph level, we need to incorporate techniques for intonation, rhythm, and varied speed, among other factors. Building on prior research, we focus on improving rhythm, variation in timing, and contextual sensitivity in speech synthesis, given their crucial roles in creating natural-sounding speech. To address these issues, we develop a novel model incorporating a hidden Markov model to predict contextual variations, a rhythm encoder to analyze prosodic features, and a continuous output layer using Markov chain-derived hidden states to generate timing predictions, all while employing spectral additive synthesis to generate the speech signal. The effectiveness of our approach in improving rhythm, timing variability, and contextual sensitivity is demonstrated through comparative analyses and evaluations on the TIMIT dataset.

We introduce and assess the projection predictive family of distributions as a means of making predictions about variables that aren't directly included in a model, enhancing its applicability to complex models, such as those utilizing non-Euclidean data representations. A means is established to project predictive uncertainty onto the model's input variables, enabling consistent uncertainty estimation both within and outside the scope of selected variables, crucial for tasks like reliable model understanding, variable selection, and robust model training. By comparing the projection predictive method with two traditional variable selection techniques, we find that it excels in retaining relevant variable selections even when dealing with non-linear relationships, thus outperforming its counterparts.

Recent research has demonstrated that Deep Neural Networks are susceptible to carefully crafted malicious inputs, known as model adversarial attacks. The current research addresses the challenge of protecting Deep Neural Networks against unknown types of attacks by employing input data analysis. A proposed method leverages a generative adversarial network to model the characteristics of potentially malicious data and employs a predicted penalty during training to enhance the robustness of the network. Experimental results confirm that this method successfully enhances the robustness of Deep Neural Networks against model adversarial attacks without any prior knowledge of the attack type, and also demonstrates minimal impact on the network's normal data accuracy.

Climate change communication is hindered by various factors, including the prevalence of conspiracy theories on social media. To gain insight into the social dynamics surrounding conspiracy theories, this research examines patterns of conspiracy-related postings on Twitter in relation to climate change beliefs. By analyzing a substantial dataset of climate change-related tweets, researchers found evidence supporting the hypothesis that individuals who do not believe in climate change are more inclined to engage with conspiracy theories, particularly those related to climate change. Furthermore, research revealed that some theories, such as the flat earth, consistently gain support from diverse groups, whereas others, such as the climate scam, receive backing from individuals who express beliefs in climate change as well as other theories. This study demonstrates the value of social media analysis in uncovering the various ways in which climate change is discussed online, identifying distinct groups, and measuring their relative influence.

A study focused on the production of dark matter in proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV has been carried out using data collected by the ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Data collection spanned 31.9 fb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity from runs in 2016 and 2018. Research involved searching for dark matter that interacts through the Higgs boson, resulting in the detection of two scalar and pseudoscalar mediators with masses less than 125 GeV. The investigation of vector mediators spanning masses from 200 to 2000 GeV revealed no significant evidence of the dark matter described in the model. Additionally, constraints were imposed on the dark matter-Higgs boson coupling strength for dark matter particles weighing between 20 and 120 GeV, and these limits were then compared to those established by searches for dark matter that occurs directly.

Given an n-exangulated category with specified properties, we establish that it satisfies Auslander-Reiten-Serre duality if and only if it possesses certain duality-based angles. We also determine a specific condition necessary for the presence of Serre duality. Assuming duality exists, we establish a one-to-one correspondence involving a bijection and specific category characteristics.

I develop methods for analyzing data from experiments that measure multiple treatment outcomes in observational data. These methods utilize data from randomized trials that employed the same treatment concepts to establish the statistical properties of each treatment effect. By exploiting variation in the trial design, such as differences in sample sizes and distribution of assignments, to enhance the statistical significance of estimates. The proposed techniques can also effectively reduce bias through "non-linear" adjustments to baseline estimates without requiring linearity assumptions. The new methods are demonstrated through an examination of research on how individuals respond to financial incentives.

To advance our understanding of matter's properties and potential connections to dark matter, researchers need high-intensity beams of antiparticles. Although antiproton production in fixed-target experiments is feasible, generating significant beams of positrons, antineutrons, and antineutrons is more challenging. We propose a new approach, using a high-intensity proton beam and a high-quality magnetic channel, to create abundant antineutrons and positrons in a target. These antiparticles can then be directed into experimental setups for scattering studies, where they can interact with nuclear targets, with an intensity that could surpass current limits and reveal new insights into anomalous forces, dark matter, and the fundamental forces of nature.

Recent numerical simulations of hierarchical triple systems have revealed complex dynamics involving accretion disks.  This research aims to provide a theoretical framework for understanding and predicting the characteristics of accretion disks in these systems.  We developed a model to calculate the differential accretion rate onto the components of a hierarchical triple system, which is then used to inform predictions of accretion disk behavior.  Results from this study show that differential accretion is highly influenced by the mass ratio between the components, with certain mass combinations leading to unstable orbits and varied accretion patterns.  Specifically, when the outer body is significantly more massive than the inner pair, long-lasting, periodic oscillations in accretion rates may be observed.  However, equal-mass systems tend to exhibit erratic and highly variable accretion patterns.  We propose that observations of accretion disks in hierarchical triple systems can provide valuable insights into their underlying dynamics, and that future space-based telescaves have the potential to verify our model's predictions.

This paper examines flat spacetimes with intrinsic properties, as potential models for understanding the universe's evolution. We demonstrate that such spacetimes can be constructed through the conformal rescaling of a standard, uniformly expanding universe model. Our analysis focuses on a specific class of spacetimes, utilizing a multiple Weyl space framework to develop various configurations. These configurations include both spatially homogeneous and not homogeneous scenarios, which are examined for their potential to generate multiple Big Bang singularities at different points in time, unlike the singularities that typically occur simultaneously in the standard Big Bang model.

This paper presents a novel task known as Image Segmentation by Image Restoration, which involves distinguishing real images from manipulated ones. Currently, most segmentation methods focus on manipulating high-quality images, which are typically distinct from the low-quality images produced by common manipulation tools such as copy-move manipulations that occur when a camera's image is shifted by one pixel. Our proposed framework addresses this limitation by effectively combining the segmentation capabilities of image restoration models with those of image segmentation models. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the copy-move manipulation detection benchmark, demonstrating a high accuracy of 96.6% on the CMCD benchmark.

Active Galactic Nuclei black holes may have their mass and spin deduced from the characteristics of their electromagnetic spectrum, specifically the position of the broad optical/UV line profile. A new method has been developed to analyze this profile using a relativity ray-tracing code to create a library of simulated lines that correspond to various mass, spin, and black hole distance values. By applying machine learning algorithms to these codes, researchers can create models that can accurately identify key parameters, and also create control samples to verify the accuracy of the models. An analysis shows that the models can accurately identify key parameters in a range of values, with high levels of accuracy, and may have the potential to be used in real-world scenarios to identify the characteristics of Active Galactic Nuclei black holes.

Creating accurate and efficient emulators of novel computing systems poses a significant challenge. To address this issue, we introduce Neuron, an open-source emulator designed for novel neuromorphic systems. This emulator leverages a functional Verilog one-liner to describe the target system, enabling the rapid development of custom instruction sets and memory hierarchies. Neuron's accuracy is validated by comparing its results with a trusted gold-standard emulator, revealing near-perfect agreement in result accuracy (99.97%) and execution time predictions (99.64%). We demonstrate Neuron's utility by designing and emulating different program execution strategies for the Fugaku supercomputer, including a novel approach called Stride, which achieves a significant speedup of 1.72x over the original implementation.

A solar type-I noise storm is an intense collection of radio bursts spanning frequencies from 100 MHz to over 300 MHz. These storms are typically observed in the decimeter to decameter wave ranges. Using the Radio Spectroscopy of the Sun experiment on board the RHESSI spacecraft, we analyzed the evolution of a storm occurring on August 20, 2002, between 14:00:00 and 14:30:00 UT. The analysis revealed two distinct evolution patterns, associated with a microflare event. The first pattern showed two frequency peaks gradually decreasing, while the second displayed a continuous decline. Both patterns were likely caused by electron interactions with an expanding shock wave in a smaller-scale structure. The rate of change of this structure was calculated to be between 100 and 200 km per second.

A compact and cost-effective magneto-optical trap has been designed, 
utilizing an open magnetic circuit design to generate and detect atom beams. 
Two pairs of superconducting coils are employed to create a broad area for 
capturing and detecting atom beams at perpendicular directions. 
Our experiment successfully captured and measured beam intensity distributions 
of a neutral $^{85}$Rb atom beam using a detected pixel camera, 
along with a simulated detection pattern that matched our experimental results.

The spherically symmetric fallback rate following a symmetric stellar explosion can be described by a well-known equation derived by Butler (1979) and Nakamura (1983). However, in real scenarios, the falling gas possesses angular momentum, causing the accretion process to occur via a rotating disk, rather than purely spherical symmetry. We have developed an analytical model for disk accretion, taking into consideration feedback from radiation pressure on dust and gas, which can significantly impact the mass accretion rate, particularly at later times. Model predictions reveal that for certain initial conditions, such as low initial mass and high mass density ratios, the mass accretion rate can decrease more rapidly than previously predicted by earlier models, by up to two orders of magnitude, and this effect is most pronounced around 100 days following the explosion, when fallback rates are typically around 10^-4 solar masses per year.

The probability of (de-)excitation and photon emission is examined for a non-relativistic, moving atom interacting with its surrounding quantum field near a large, flat conductive surface. These processes are analyzed through reduced Dirac and Wick rotations in momentum space, leading to modified equations that incorporate the boundary conditions imposed by the surface. Unlike previous models, our surface-derived equations naturally accommodate the surface's translational symmetry, allowing seamless integration of surface and plane-wave modes without artificial approximations.

A significant population of massive stars in nearby galaxies is observed in isolated environments outside of dense clusters.  The existence of these stars has been historically attributed to massive stars forming in low-density regions with properties similar to those of high-density star-forming areas.  We have developed a theoretical framework, based on the application of the Monte-Carlo code, to accurately simulate 3D and time-dependent changes in low-density, massive molecular cloud fragments.  These simulations demonstrate the capability of this model to generate star clusters that accurately match observed features in the Carina Nebula.  Specifically, our model is in line with previous observations of H-alpha and near-infrared spectra, which supports the theory of massive star formation within isolated environments.  Furthermore, the simulations reveal that a combination of unidirectional and random motion patterns can be used to generate a distribution of star cluster ages that is consistent with observed data.  As a result, the model is a valuable tool for understanding the complex dynamics of star cluster formation and can be applied to various galaxies to uncover hidden cluster populations.

This paper investigates the normalized ground state solution for a specified biharmonic Choquard type equation. By applying various techniques from recent research and a specific minimization approach, we demonstrate the existence of a fundamental solution for this normalized problem.

Degraded handwritten documents, which are affected by factors such as discolouration, stains, and tears, often become unreadable and require restoration. To address this issue, we propose an end-to-end approach for restoring single-page handwritten documents using generative adversarial networks. By utilizing labeled data for image enhancement, we can effectively restore page-level handwritten documents while minimizing the need for annotated images through a new weak supervision technique for segmenting modern written texts. Experimental results on the RDW867 dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in producing visually coherent restored documents.

The rapid growth of the internet of things (IoT) has led to an unprecedented explosion in data generation, which has severely tested data processing capabilities. This problem is particularly pronounced in countries like India, where a large population combined with an expanding digital infrastructure has led to an even greater data overload. In the context of this study, we investigate the effectiveness of using optical character recognition (OCR) and string manipulation techniques to extract and OCR the relevant information from machine-readable ID card images in a data-driven manner. Our approach utilizes conventional and advanced OCR methods to convert ID card images into text, then leverages string manipulation to accurately extract key details such as surnames, names, dates of birth, and OCR the relevant information from the relevant ID card images in a manner that is both efficient and scalable.

In vehicle-to-vehicle communications, the OQAM-OFDM system is commonly used, and effective channel tracking is crucial for high data transfer rates. Due to the limited number of pilots available, we propose a new method for estimating channel coefficients, which utilizes both pilot and non-pilot subcarriers. This new approach utilizes a sparse reconstruction technique, which can accurately track changes in the vehicle's movement and adapt to its patterns, using previously collected information. Through theoretical analysis and practical testing, we demonstrate that our proposed technique results in better channel estimation accuracy compared to conventional methods, especially in high mobility situations. Furthermore, we show that using our approach allows for the reduction of pilots, which can lead to improved power efficiency.

The task of automatically assigning colors to images, given only grayscale data, has been a longstanding challenge in machine learning for a long time. Recent advances in machine learning, particularly deep learning, have led to a surge in interest in colorization tasks, with applications spanning art restoration and medical imaging to DPY and other problems. Despite these developments, the potential of using domain adaptation techniques to further improve colorization methods remains underexplored. We conducted experiments using several state-of-the-art models, including GAN-based approaches and a recent domain adaptation technique on two datasets with differing domains to investigate the potential benefits of adapting these models to improve colorization performance. Our results demonstrate that combining a non-convex optimization approach with supervised learning on encyclopedic paintings and outdoor scenes datasets yields colorization performances superior to traditional methods, particularly when colors are sparse.

We've developed a novel numerical scheme to efficiently calculate Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) weights without relying on stochastic gradient descent. Based on the Universal Approximation Theorem, our method deterministically achieves precise values for weights, allowing for seamless integration with existing ANN frameworks and the use of various non-differentiable loss functions. Furthermore, our method's time and space complexities are both linear, making it a practical and flexible method for weight optimization.

The ECFA Early Career Researcher's panel started representing the interests of young researchers within the ECFA community in January 2021. Throughout its first two years of operation, the panel developed its organizational framework, defined its objectives, coordinated with other ECFA panels and external groups like the CERN ERC, and prepared a comprehensive report detailing its recommendations for future accelerator developments. This report outlines the observations and strategies that would support the full realization of the potential offered by next-generation accelerators.

We've discovered line waves that can form at the boundary between two customized segments, and these waves possess non-orthogonal properties and lack an associated radiation pattern. This phenomenon can be effectively showcased through metasurfaces that control dual electromagnetic structures. These line waves can be stimulated by perpendicular and oblique polarized plane waves and can be visualized through enhanced propagation patterns and concentrated power. Furthermore, these line waves can be utilized to convey and concentrate signals, and our theoretical model has been successfully validated through numerical experiments.

One of the most promising areas in technology, multi-agent learning, holds significant potential to revolutionize various sectors such as agriculture, manufacturing, and healthcare. To address complex system design problems, researchers employ multi-agent learning, a computational framework that can address intricate optimization issues. This concept is particularly appealing due to its potential to provide versatile solutions for interlinked problems. This work delves into its application in robotic systems, highlighting the challenges it presents and proposing innovative approaches to overcome them. To facilitate interdisciplinary collaboration, we offer a unified definition of multi-agent learning, integrating perspectives from the fields of computer science and engineering. This report provides an in-depth exploration of the field, reviewing existing literature, investigating potential applications, and providing an outlook on where multi-agent learning might lead in the future.

A new bias-corrected method is proposed to estimate parameters in a mean absolute deviation model at specific points, with improved accuracy demonstrated through numerical simulations and real-world data analysis.

The task of relation extraction is a fundamental aspect of natural language understanding that has been extensively addressed through the use of supervised and unsupervised approaches, yet attempts to develop unsupervised methods that operate without requiring any annotations have largely gone unnoticed. Our proposed Relational Joint Inference Framework (RJIF) addresses this gap by simultaneously performing joint inference on relations and sub-events within domains where relation definitions are unavailable. Utilizing a novel model that incorporates non-negative matrix factorization, we demonstrate its efficacy through experiments conducted on the OG220 domain, showcasing its ability to uncover both hidden semantic structures and functional patterns in data.

The Analytical-spectral method is used in N-dimensional space to solve the linearized Schrödinger equation for quarkonium, taking into account the finite range of the interaction potential, which is limited by the Debye length. By applying a suitable transformation to the Schrödinger equation, its solutions can be obtained in terms of the Laguerre polynomials. Consequently, the energy levels of quarkonium in N-dimensional space are calculated. These results show that anisotropy significantly impacts the dissociation of quarkonium, with the effect increasing with higher values of N. Moreover, anisotropy generally leads to a lower dissociation temperature compared to isotropic conditions. Nevertheless, under certain circumstances, anisotropy may result in an increase in the dissociation temperature. These findings imply that anisotropy influences the quarkonium ground state's behavior in N-dimensional space.

Our study focused on the magnetic properties of Tb3RuO7 using neutron powder diffraction to determine its crystal structure. We discovered that in a temperature range below 15 K, the sub-lattice magnetic structures of the Ta1 and Ta2 positions display different ordering patterns, which eventually synchronize above this temperature range at 8 K. We calculated the Ir1 and Tb3 magnetic moments, and the findings show that the sub-lattice magnetic structures of Tb and Ru are almost entirely ordered, with a negligible moment for Tb3. We proposed a magnetic structure model for Tb3RuO7 based on its magnetic properties, and the study indicated that in a temperature range below 8 K, the proposed magnetic model is in agreement with our findings.

Machine learning, particularly artificial neural networks, excels at processing signals, yet its effectiveness is hampered by high computational costs associated with its components. A novel solution involves developing a more efficient representation for images and videos using memory-efficient machine learning techniques that incorporate multiple layers of functionality, enhancing effectiveness while maintaining machine processability. To test this concept, we have created a simple but effective architecture comprising two layers of functionality, and applied it successfully to binary classification of binary 32x32 images, 16x16 videos, and 8x8 binary frames, while also applying the technique to neural network compression. Our innovative approach offers an effective alternative to traditional data reduction methods, such as quantization and pruning, and can potentially be applied in resource-constrained environments, such as mobile devices, while also serving as a viable technique for neural network compression.

Traditional methods of covariate-shift adaptation utilize unlabelled data to adjust model parameters toward their optimal values, effectively accommodating various degree of distributional shifts, whether marked or unmarked.  Nonetheless, integrating adaptation techniques with semi-supervised learning can yield significant improvements, especially when considering changes in both parameters and distribution simultaneously, as demonstrated in our research.  Semi-supervised learning techniques have been extensively investigated, with numerous outstanding open problems, and our objective is to explore their potential use in adaptation, highlighting unique opportunities that arise from combining these two areas.  To achieve this goal, we outline a distinct classification of change detection methods that are particularly relevant to adaptation and highlight their underlying principles, before delving into specific proposed methods, evaluating their performance with empirical results, and then consider the implications of our findings and potential future research directions.

Despite its impressive task-specific performance, the inner workings of deep learning systems remain elusive, characterized by intricate geometric structures that defy straightforward interpretation, according to traditional mathematical standards. In an effort to shed light on this complexity, researchers employed sophisticated geometric tools, discovering that certain aspects of deep learning, such as convolutional neural networks, can be modeled using Lie group structures, neural ordinary differential equations, and certain deep learning architectures, submanifolds within their respective Lie groups, whereas other systems, like ResNets, exhibit the structural equivalencies of parallel transport along paths in their respective manifolds. This discovery not only clarifies the inner workings of these systems, but also enables researchers to leverage well-established geometric and group-theoretic theories to inform deep learning design, ultimately leading to enhanced understanding and potential breakthroughs in the field.

We consider the field extension $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{d},\omega)$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ for a positive square-free integer $d$, where $\omega$ represents a cubic root of unity. It is established that infinite subsets of integers from the set of positive square-free values of $d$ result in principal ideals of the extension's ring of integers being generatable solely by elements from rings of integers of subfields of the extension, specifically $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d})$ and $\mathbb{Q}(\omega)$. The analysis also identifies constraints on generators that can initiate such generic elements.

A novel method is introduced to integrate distinct types of variables within a single deep neural network classifier. The classification task is framed in the context of jet substructure tagging, and a multi-stage technique named from-TL is presented to tag Higgs bosons that decay into two tau leptons. The method incorporates established classification indicators derived from tau templates and enhances it using a DNN. The performance gains achieved through this method surpass the limitations imposed by quantum fluctuations in the measurement process.

For every positive integer r, a specific kind of Stirling number is used to count how many ways a set can be divided into a specified number of non-empty subsets, where each subset contains at least r elements. We're introducing a variation of these Stirling numbers, which represents their extreme forms, reducing to well-known cases when r equals one. This paper seeks to establish formulas linking these variations together.

Eighty sets of layer groups were examined, each consisting of four types: ordinary and double, as well as gray single and double. Layer group properties allowed for the efficient computation of relevant physical characteristics using symbolic methods, which in turn. exploited the eightfold symmetry. This symmetry. held true for low-lying electronic and vibrational states, as well. as, when spin-orbit interactions were absent, for certain double particle states with zero total. spin.

Momentum operators are explored in the context of intrinsically curved manifolds, specifically focusing on compact-radius manifolds of positive sectional curvature, such as the sphere $S^n$ with its standard metric, the complex projective space $\mathbb{C}P^n$ with its Fubini-Study metric, and $\mathbb{H}P^n$ with its normalized metric. It is demonstrated that the square of the symmetric, unbounded, self-adjoint, positively defined, Laplace-Beltrami operator $\Delta^2$ has a discrete spectrum with an infimum that is strictly greater than zero. By utilizing the resolvent of $\Delta^2$, an unbounded, positively defined, strictly contractive, symmetric, and invertible Jensen operator $Q(\lambda)$ for $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$ is introduced, based on the spectral theorem in ( \S4). The resolvent is described in terms of Bessel functions of the first and second kind in ( \S5). The contractive property of $Q(\lambda)$, its spectral representation, and the convergence of the contractive sequence to a Dirac delta function at $\lambda = 0$ are investigated in ( \S6). The relationship between $Q(\lambda)$ and the Fourier transform, as well as the contrast property, is discussed in ( \S7). The uncertainty principle for $\Delta^2$ is established in ( \S8). The $\

A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant. Our research focuses on developing an efficient method to counteract this expense by leveraging a neural network to predict the determinant. We have applied this method to a two-dimensional model of interacting fermions, demonstrating that it outperforms existing approaches by reducing the computational cost and effectively addressing the sign problem even beyond half-filling.

We introduce a composite Higgs model based on the Dinar group, where the field that forms the Higgs is an complex scalar field, different from the recent models that use a pseudo Goldstone boson. This model is based on a setup where a complex scalar field is introduced in the invariant sector of the coset space. The model is based on the idea that the symmetry group Dinar D52 is broken down to Dinar D34, where the fields that are invariant under Dinar D34 include the complex scalar field. This model is based on the idea that the symmetry group Dinar D34 is a subgroup of the symmetry group Dinar D52. This model is based on the idea that the symmetry group Dinar D52 is broken down to a subgroup that is invariant under the field that forms the Higgs. The use of Virtual-Physical Perceptual Manipulations, like redirected walking and haptics, extends VR experiences beyond conventional physical and perceptual boundaries by reinterpreting them. This paper explores the manipulation of user perceptions in VR to enhance interactivity, taking an interdisciplinary approach that blends insights from psychology, engineering, and the philosophy of manipulation. Our analysis identifies and distinguishes four types of VPPMs based on their objectives, targeting users' senses, sub-conscious responses, or redirecting their physical movements. This classification helps to enhance our comprehension of both existing VPPMs and the potential for unexplored manipulations, highlighting opportunities for innovative applications and enhancements to user experiences in VR environments.

To assess various approaches to expanding language coverage, we integrate German and Korean into BigScience's large-scale, 1.3 billion parameter multilingual language model, initially trained on 13 languages. Our study focuses on key factors influencing model adaptability for new languages and weighs the computational expense against potential performance gains.

Recent observations from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array have revealed that young binary stars have a mass ratio distribution similar to that of older binaries.  This suggests a common formation process, which can be explored through numerical simulations of core fragmentation.  Our model assumes that binary fragments form from the irregular infall of a rotating parent core and calculates how many cores of varying sizes break apart to create binaries.  Results show that variations in binary mass ratios correspond to fluctuations in the mass of the parent core, which we used to determine the distribution of binary formation masses.  When considering realistic distributions of binary properties, our findings suggest that binary systems with lower masses are more likely to be formed from the fragmentation of heavier parent cores.  Moreover, as the total mass of the core increases, so does the mass of the formed binary, which can lead to the creation of ternary systems through further fragmentation.  These trends are consistent across various binary populations observed in different star-forming regions, which in turn are influenced by the properties of the surrounding molecular cloud.

This research introduces the m-arcsinh Kernel 'k' Kernel 'r' Kernel 'FastIndependent Component Analysis' (m-arK-FastICA) approach, an upgraded version of the 'k' 'r' FastICA algorithm tailored for extracting features from unstable datasets containing anomalies. Unlike existing methods that focus on specific types of distortions, m-arK-FastICA is designed to handle a broader range of irregularities using a combination of arithmetic and hyperbolic functions in its optimization process. Furthermore, this study presents modifications to the standard FastICA algorithm to increase its efficiency, along an alternative approach based on the 'e' function ('esICA') for an alternative solution to maximizing entropy. Experimental results from both simulated and actual data analyses demonstrate the superiority of m-arK-FastICA, as well as the proposed entropy-based method, over existing techniques in various conditions.

This paper builds on existing research regarding the limitations of certain logical systems in determining graph isomorphism, particularly for systems like the bounded-degree extended polynomial calculus. The key finding is that any polynomial system with a degree limit can identify non-isomorphic graphs in CP-time, which has significant implications: it allows such a system to process specific graph problems in NP-time, even after degree restrictions. In contrast, distinguishing graphs in such a system generally requires time in bounded-degree extended polynomial calculus. The study also explores how a PC system can effectively solve specific decision problems in NP through a degree-based approach.

A subring collection in a ring $R$ that when multiplied element-wise by any other subring produces all possible products within the ring is known as a covering number. The ring's associative and unital properties remain unchanged during this process. The concept of a unique maximal nilpotent ring, a ring in which all products eventually become zero, allows us to define the first covering number for the ring $R$. The research focuses on determining the value of this first covering number for the ring $R$. The study extends to the ring of integers modulo $p^n$, denoted as $\mathbb{Z}_{p^{\mathfrak{n}}}$, where the value of its first covering number, $\mathfrak{c}_1(\mathbb{Z}_{p^{\mathfrak{n}}})$, has been determined and illustrated with numerical examples.

Social media platforms have become notorious for spreading fake news and misleading information, an issue exacerbated by the difficulty humans face in verifying the vast amount of content they encounter daily. To address this challenge, automated fact-checking systems are essential, yet they struggle to address the preliminary step of pinpointing relevant claims. Our study introduces an innovative approach to pre-claim detection, which leverages the power of contextually-aware aspect detection and subjective opinion classification. By breaking down claims into distinct aspects, our model identifies the key adjectives that convey the speaker's sentiment, effectively categorizing them as subjective, thereby facilitating a more accurate and efficient fact-checking process.

Identifying trending social media events in real-time across various locations is crucial for tracking emerging topics.传统的 approaches rely on unstructured data analysis, which often overlooks the significance of structured information like Twitter API callsenges. This paper presents a novel method that leverages Twitter API callsenges to accurately detect and prioritize events. It also offers a visual interface to display the results. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in capturing events related to the Olympics, World Cup, and specific locations like Hurricane Matthew and Florida fires, all while maintaining low computational costs. The associated code and interface are available on GitHub.

We've introduced a novel method of analysis, the weighted skew-spectrum, which combines information from various scales to provide more precise estimates of cosmological parameters and effective Neutrino Mass. This technique shows improved accuracy in determining these parameters when applied to tomographic weak lensing data and the Large Scale Structure of the universe within a framework of general relativity. This increased precision allows us to revisit the tension regarding Neutrino Mass by introducing more accurate parameters and providing more reliable constraints on them.

By integrating Bayesian learning into adversarial training of deep neural networks, we developed a rigorous framework for training certifiable Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs). This approach combines constraint relaxation and modified cross-entropy loss to achieve accurate BNN training, which we demonstrated leads toBNNs that are both highly competitive in performance and capable of providing reliable uncertainty estimates on test data, outperforming existing methods on CIFAR-10 under various attack scenarios.

The COVID-19 pandemic caused widespread disruption, and false information spread rapidly on social media. To better understand the social dynamics driving the dissemination of rumors, we developed a data-driven approach to track the evolution of online rumors in China. By analyzing online content, we identified key themes and traced the development of rumors over time. Our results showed that rumors initially focused on the virus's rapid spread, but later shifted to include beliefs in a man-made outbreak and links to 5G technology. These early rumors peaked within two weeks but gradually declined. To tackle the issue, distinguishing true from false information remains crucial. Our analysis also reveals the social networks promoting and hindering rumor dissemination. Influential figures who disseminate rumors include celebrities, but those who question them are experts like doctors and journalists. Notably, celebrities and fans played a significant role in the peak of rumor spread, whereas discussions led by experts and journalists contributed to reducing rumor prevalence. Our findings can inform more effective public information strategies to combat rumor dissemination.

This study investigates the effectiveness of pixel classification in high-dimensional images with reduced dimensions using three compression techniques. These compression methods are principal component analysis, autoencoder, and sparsifying transformation, and their impact on hyperspectral image pixels is examined. By applying these techniques to a comprehensive dataset of 2,112 hyperspectral images, we analyze the relationship between compression rate and pixel classification accuracy for various classifiers and datasets. The experimental results reveal that the compression structure significantly influences pixel classification performance and that different images respond uniquely to various compression methods. Consequently, an optimal compression method exists for each image type, and this study provides a framework to evaluate and compare various compression methods by analyzing their effect on pixel classification accuracy across diverse datasets.

Neural networks, characterized by their substantial number of parameters, often face
interpretation difficulties. In an effort to address this, researchers have
investigated the lottery ticket hypothesis, suggesting the existence of subsets of
parameters within these networks that can achieve optimal performance when used
exclusively. Our study aims to validate this theory by examining its applicability
to supervised image classification tasks, specifically using the widely recognized
MNIST dataset. By applying various pruning methods and comparing the performance
of different approaches, our findings provide notable insights into the nature of
these sub-networks and their capacity for efficient model training.

A novel prediction method, referred to as ProCS, has been introduced to calculate amide proton chemical shifts for proteins with sequences longer than 10 residues. ProCS utilizes a bidirectional transformer architecture, trained through an unsupervised approach based on a comprehensive dataset of experimentally determined human protein sequences and their corresponding chemical shifts. The method's success in generating realistic ProCS outputs for various proteins, including those containing post-translational modifications, outperforms existing protein structure prediction techniques in predicting chemical shifts, highlighting its potential utility in stabilizing the AlphaFold2 model and aiding in the investigation of protein and complex structures.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is a critical decision in the lossless compression of data and supervised classification tasks. Despite the prevalence of cross-entropy loss in classification problems, our investigation reveals that alternative loss functions can yield more efficient results. We introduce a universal approach to loss function optimization that significantly enhances accuracy when combined with stochastic gradient descent. Specifically, in 2D image classification challenges, custom-optimized loss functions consistently outperform conventional cross-entropy, achieving improvements of up to 1%. When applied to existing image datasets, we demonstrate that tuning the loss function can lead to substantial reductions in numerical discrepancies, with values decreasing by as much as two orders of magnitude.

We have created an educational resource that encompasses various aspects of many-body correlations, with a focus on the parquet theory framework. This comprehensive document covers fundamental concepts and advanced topics including local and non-local correlations, the application of diagrams, and the integration of different approximations within the parquet model. Additionally, it discusses advanced parquet-type theories that emphasize non-local correlations.

The process of exciton condensation, which may occur through Bose-Einstein condensation, is a phenomenon of significant interest in solid-state physics. However, achieving this process in a system that does not have an exciton drive is extremely difficult. We propose a method to induce exciton condensation without an exciton drive by utilizing light, using it to drive the system into a highly correlated regime. We study a slab of semimetal exposed to a strong magnetic field, where the interplay between light and matter can result in exciton condensation, evident through the emergence of a temperature-dependent energy gap. Furthermore, we find that the partially occupied excitations display a unique property, where their momentum distribution exhibits two distinct peaks.

In the US, numerous communities utilize volunteer-based systems to process and analyze reports of neighborhood safety incidents. Although these communities have developed effective processes to minimize reporting fatigue, there is a significant gap in analyzing emotional support provided by system operators, known as dispatchers. A large dataset from RedFlagNetwork, comprising over 100,000 interactions between dispatchers and users in 2020, was analyzed to investigate how dispatchers respond to report submitters. Our findings reveal substantial variation in dispatchers' use of emotional support language, highlighting a strong correlation between emotional support and higher user response rates. By utilizing natural language processing, we identified specific phrases that dispatchers used to encourage users to complete their profiles and resubmit reports, showcasing the importance of emotional support in reducing user fatigue. Ultimately, our research underscores the necessity of integrating emotional support into system design to mitigate reporting fatigue and improve community engagement.

To analyze the impact of external pressure on doped topological insulator Bi$_2$Se$_3$, we used terahertz spectroscopy to analyze superconducting properties in both bulk and surface regions under pressure up to 5 kbar. Our research revealed that the superconducting gap in Bi$_2$Se$_3$ exhibits isotropic behavior, with our analysis consistent with a nodal superconducting gap under pressure. Furthermore, our temperature-dependent measurements revealed that the superconducting transition in Bi$_2$Se$_3$ exhibits an abrupt change, with our analysis indicating that the superconducting transition is caused by electron-phonon interaction in this material.

Label-efficient active learning models play a crucial role in supervising the training of large AI models by reducing labeling costs. Current methods for active learning sample data points using either a probability distribution or heuristic rules, which only consider individual instance uncertainties and overlook the interactions between them. This paper introduces a new approach that views uncertainty as a game theory problem, formulating a utility function to select labeled instances under a predetermined budget. By utilizing a Bayesian game to model uncertainties, we develop a utility function that balances the uncertainties of multiple data instances and employs adversarial training to find the optimal labeling budget allocation strategy. Unlike previous methods, our utility function is universally applicable to various teachers and models, and we validate its effectiveness through comprehensive unit tests and user studies, which showcase its performance on multiple datasets and its robustness.

To study how music has evolved over time, we need a method to quantify differences between songs from various periods, and our research introduces the concept of "Loudness Complexity" to achieve this goal. Firstly, we developed the average loudness complexity of a song as a metric that effectively captures the time-varying intricacies between songs, and our findings reveal that this complexity has increased by 20% from the 1960s to now. Building on this discovery, we created the MCVC model, which combines the $M$-th order Volterra series, Variational Autoencoders, and Cross-spectral analysis, to model the cross-spectral pseudo-battery function. MCVC demonstrates a superior performance in modeling the characteristics of music compared to existing music modeling techniques. Ultimately, we employed the MCVC model to model the evolution of pop music over time, taking into consideration individual song characteristics, and our research provides novel insights into music trends that were previously overlooked.

A novel class of random partitions of the natural numbers is described by an equational process, extending a method previously studied in papers [9] and stochastically analyzed in journal articles published in 2015 and 2018 within the Annals of Applied Probability. In this framework, an infinite sequence of numbers occurs and for each new entry a probability is calculated to either append it to an existing block or initiate a new block based on an underlying completely bounded measure valued in the interval of 0 to 1 to the power of one, denoted as $\nu \in \mathcal{M}_{\text{cb}}([0,1])$. This describes the conditions under which the process takes place and leads to natural non-exchangeable partitions of the natural numbers. The research examines these conditions under which a probability measure over the set of non-exchangeable partitions can be constructed and characterized. In particular, the study identifies conditions under which a probability measure can be determined on a specific set of partitions of the interval of 0 to 1 denoted as $[0,1]$ and the conditions under which this probability measure is concentrated on a specific subset of partitions of the natural numbers for which each block is an interval of natural numbers. The study extends key combinatorial results from partitions of the natural numbers to non-exchangeable partitions of the interval of 0 to 1 denoted as $[0,1]$.

Prawitz's classic investigation into the Pruning Method for intuitionistic natural deduction has been extended to the realm of inductive definition of functions. The formulation has been achieved through the introduction of a new type of terms, and the associated proof has been presented, but interestingly the introduction of these new terms has not influenced the original proof's integrity. The specific example provided is the Pruning Method for the Kripke-Jayaraman system, and the introduction of these new terms can be applied to other systems as well.

A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. Through data visualization, the outputs of a latent variable model are displayed, enabling human interaction on a visual interface, thereby effectively enhancing the quality of human feedback. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves performance equivalent to full annotation in both efficiency and accuracy, paving the way for a more practical implementation in real-world settings.

We show that a topological space's Smyth powerspace is core-compact if and only if the original space has local compactness. Consequently, this implies the Smyth powerspace does not uniformly preserve core-compact properties.

We're investigating singular vorticities in ideal two-dimensional fluids with specific properties derived from point vortices and vortex sheets. These characteristics are defined by measures concentrated on compact subsets of the plane that don't include the origin. This study builds on existing theories to develop a new framework for the precise weak solution, enabling the application of Young measure theory to a specific first-order Hamilton-Jacobi equation. This application reveals the precise solution's regularity and provides insights into the associated flow fields. This work also contributes to the understanding of ideal 2D fluids by offering a novel class of singular vorticities and the associated precise vorticity dynamics.

The Average Treatment Effect, particularly when treated as a parameter dependent on an underlying population, is estimated through flexible nonparametric methods known as estimators AIPW and nAIPW. These estimators are built from consistent, first-order for the original AIPW, but exhibit different behavior in terms of bias and inference properties. Despite these differences, both estimators maintain orthogonality and invariance under transformation properties. In addition, these estimators are now accompanied by corresponding functional estimators that can evaluate the treatment effect at specific points.

The anomalies of lepton flavor universality violations found in particle decays have led to speculation about the existence of novel physics. Among potential candidates, the neutral scalar particle denoted as $\tau$ has garnered significant interest due to its anticipated large production cross-section at the Large Hadron Collider. In this research, we conduct an in-depth examination of $\tau$-mediated interactions within the context of the $B$-meson factory environment, specifically analyzing the process $B^0_s\to\tau^+\tau^-$. Our investigation encompasses $\tau$'s impact on various angular observables and relevant observables that can be measured in future $B$-factories, revealing that $\tau$ model can effectively explain the experimental data for the observed anomalies in the described decay. Furthermore, we determine the region in parameter space that is consistent with current $B$-factories' measurements and is expected to be constrained by upcoming $B$-factories within approximately one year.

A fundamental challenge in atmospheric circulation modeling is simulating the development of cyclogenesis, the process by which storms are formed, in a top-down approach that begins with a simplified, featureless ocean. The intricate dynamics of storm creation, however, rely heavily on small-scale interactions, raising the question of whether such models can accurately replicate this process without a representation of these interactions, particularly in cases where the resolution is insufficient to capture them directly. The use of turbulence closures, which attempt to account for these small-scale effects, is essential in a variety of scientific and engineering simulations, yet their performance at different scales remains uncertain. In particular, the performance of turbulence closures in generating realistic atmospheric circulation is not well-understood. The evaluation of these closures is complicated by the diverse range of parameters that can be adjusted, each of which may have a significant impact on the resulting simulations. The ultimate goal of these simulations is to determine whether they can produce a general circulation that matches observed weather patterns, such as the jet stream and westerlies, without explicitly forcing the atmosphere with external factors. The ultimate test of a simulation's realism, however, lies in the the thermodynamic balance that must exist in a globally circulating system, where the net energy transfer from the equator to the poles must be zero. The use of turbulence closures has the potential to significantly improve the accuracy of atmospheric and oceanic simulations, but their performance and the parameters that control them must be carefully evaluated to ensure that they are producing realistic results.

A key aspect in modelling extreme events is selecting the appropriate threshold level in threshold models, which often leads to increased complexity in models and the need for higher dimensional parameter estimation. To address this limitation, we introduce a type of threshold-invariant parameter that allows us to simplify the model and reduce the number of parameters needed to be estimated. By utilizing numerical techniques, we successfully extend this simplified approach to non-linear models, providing the ability to fit a wide range of functions in place of the standard linear model. The flexibility of this method is demonstrated through data analysis of storm surges in the North Sea, providing insights into the frequency of extreme events in the region.

In the field of offline reinforcement learning, we focus on adversaries that can manipulate a fraction of data tuples, which poses a significant challenge in learning accurate policies. Our research introduces two key concepts, robust value function estimation and robust q-function estimation, to address this issue. By incorporating robust estimation, we developed an offline reinforcement learning algorithm capable of achieving a minimum return within a certain error margin, even when up to a specified proportion of data is compromised. This result marks the first robust value estimation method with sub-Gaussian estimation errors in the presence of adversarial corruption. Building on this, we established robust q-function estimation, from which another algorithm emerged, capable of achieving a minimum return within a specified error margin, which outperforms previous robust offline reinforcement learning methods by significantly reducing the sample complexity required.

This study demonstrates a logarithmic convexity linked to observability at a specific point in time for a one-dimensional heat equation under dynamic boundary conditions, leading to impulse approximate controllability in similar scenarios with dynamic boundaries. Additionally, we provide a detailed estimate for the cost of impulse control. Our research includes a step-by-step procedure for finding the impulsive control of minimal L^2-norm and supports these findings with numerical tests to verify the efficiency of the developed algorithm.

A consensus has not been reached on how to effectively detect out-of-distribution examples, especially when considering different types of changes, such as domain shifts and coverage shifts. In this study, we analyze a total of 26 methods for identifying out-of-distribution examples across four synthetic data sets designed to mimic real-world data changes. Our findings reveal that current consensus-based and density-based methods show varying levels of effectiveness depending on the type of change, with domain shifts generally favoring the former and others favoring the latter. As a result, we conclude that combining multiple methods can lead to an overall significant improvement in detecting out-of-distribution examples, across both real and synthetic data sets, as demonstrated by 10 experiments on publicly available data sets, where 8 of them showed clear evidence of this overall improvement.

Our study on artificial molecular machines, particularly artificial molecular motors, begins by establishing a fundamental understanding of their molecular motors function. We will analyze how thermal fluctuations and electric currents contribute to their operation, highlighting the significance of distinguishing between these two distinct scenarios. In the first instance, where only thermal energy is involved, the motor's operation can be modeled as a Brownian motor, driven by random movements in a thermally driven environment, constrained by asymmetric structures at the molecular level. Alternatively, in the presence of an electric current, the motor's operation can be modeled as a particle in a thermally driven environment, with the space it occupies being adiabatic in nature. Ultimately, our investigation aims to provide a basic understanding of how these factors interact to drive the operation of artificial molecular motors, which has direct implications for the development of new materials with unique properties.

Building on a previous study, we examine various notions of behavior for transducers
that relate to functions defined on infinite sequences, focusing on whether these notions are decisive regarding inclusion for different types of multi-infinite sequence functions.
We find that certain decidability results hold for specific cases, such as when one in a pair of functions has a limited set of possible outputs, but fail in other instances, including when both functions have limited possible inputs.
To address this, we introduce a specific type of restriction, where the sets of possible inputs for both functions in a query are limited to a small finite number, and provide a specific type of single-letter alphabet for which the problem becomes decisive under some but not all notions of behavior.
Additionally, we explore the relationship between different notions of behavior and provide a specific pair of functions that illustrates how certain properties are decisive under specific transducer definitions, but become non-decisive when other properties are introduced.

In this study, we investigate the concept of general convolution as an abstraction of polynomial multiplication. By considering a function $f$ that maps from a set of sizes to a group, and a set of $m$ functions that map from sizes to the same group, our goal is to compute the convolution of $f$ and each of the $m$ functions with a time complexity of $m$ times the number of sizes to a power of three-halves. Through an example involving shortest path computation in directed graphs, our results show that the problem is applicable to various scenarios, given an existing approach with time complexity $k$ times the number of sizes to a power of three-halves, our new approach achieves a speedup of a linear factor of $k$.

The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1996 was groundbreaking as it enabled detailed study of late-type dwarf spectra. Since then, our understanding of its spectrum has improved with better instruments and data analysis techniques. Despite this, a significant disagreement remains in the estimates of GJ 229B's basic properties when compared to other exoplanets and brown dwarfs. Our research employs state-of-the-art line lists and modern spectroscopic retrieval software to provide more accurate mass and atmospheric parameter estimates for GJ 229B. Our analysis indicates a mass range of 28-60 $M_{\rm J}$ and a range in temperature from 450-600 K and luminosity between $10^{-6}$ and $10^{-4}L_{\odot}$. Our results are consistent with existing literature, with our mass estimate being on the lower end of the spectrum.

To search for the possible existence of the $c$-like or $gluonball$ state $0^{--}$, we employed the QCD sum rule technique, considering an interaction Lagrangian and choosing specific quark flavors. By incorporating a mass constraint and an unusual magnetic-type Dirac structure, we found that no reasonable sum rule could be constructed, thus indicating that the $0^{--}$ exotic state is unlikely to exist below 2 GeV.

A precise measurement of the mixing-induced CP violation phase $\phi_d$ is crucial in exploring the source of matter-antimatter asymmetry, and thus a crucial component in efforts to expand our understanding of the Standard Model. The precise prediction of $\phi_d$ within the Standard Model is complicated by large uncertainties in the hadronic matrix element, and thus a direct measurement of B meson decay rates is necessary. A direct measurement of $\phi_d$ from $B^0\to K^+\pi^-$ decays is possible with the high-luminosity upgrade of the BESIII detector, and with a dataset of up to $2.5~\mathrm{ab}^{-1}$ will achieve a precision of 0.55 degrees.

Airborne transmission research focuses on the spread of diseases in crowded, indoor environments like hospitals. Research into the dynamics of virus-carrying particles in such settings requires a thorough understanding of how these particles behave. We present a novel research approach that combines laboratory experiments, numerical modeling, and theoretical analysis to investigate the flow of aerosols containing particles that mimic real-world conditions. Our experiments, which measure the concentration of these particles in various parts of an enclosed space, are validated by a concentrated fluorescence marker. We track the flow of these particles through 3D visualizations, demonstrating that their movement is influenced by factors such as air recirculation and the deposition of particles that contains the marker. By developing a model to predict particle coagulation and sedimentation, which accounts for the particles' physical properties, we obtain a model that accurately matches our experimental results, providing a framework for predicting how infectious aerosols spread in indoor environments.

We conducted a comprehensive investigation of the $\beta$-decay characteristics of isotopes situated at both the neutron-rich and proton-rich boundaries. By utilizing the interaction GXD1 within the shell-model framework, we calculated key properties such as $\beta$-decay half-lives, log ft values, and forbidden $\beta$-decay transitions for these boundary isotopes. Our study encompassed 26 cases, focusing on neutron-rich $^{36}$Si, $^{42}$Ca, $^{62}$Ni and various even-proton isotones, as well as proton-rich $^{122}$Sn and various odd-Z isotopes. Our results were extensively compared with available experimental data to assess their accuracy. Additionally, we made efforts to predict $\beta$-decay properties for under-studied isotopes lacking experimental data.

Double-sided auctions are commonly used in financial markets to facilitate matching. 
Recently, researchers have explored the concept of multi-quantity trade requests within this framework. 
Building upon this progress, our work introduces a novel model that incorporates order cancellation and multi-quantity trade requests. 
The paper presents a data structure based on trees to quickly identify cancellable requests and their matching outcomes. 
Experimental results demonstrate that our method significantly enhances the efficiency of financial trading systems.

We utilize heavy quark effective theory to investigate the $F$-wave bottom mesons, applying both theoretical and experimental data to calculate the mass of these mesons. Additionally, by examining the decay widths of bottom mesons, we derive upper limits on their corresponding coupling values. Our research further includes constructing Regge trajectories in the planes of angular momentum (J) and squared mass (M^2), yielding outcomes that align neatly with Regge theory predictions. Notably, the calculated Regge slopes for vectors and scalars show slight discrepancies, aligning independently at 0.39 GeV^2 and 0.41 GeV^2, respectively, which is a marginally lower value than the pion lattice QCD measurement of 0.44 GeV^2.

Michal Szabados initially proposed a theory in his doctoral dissertation. In this current paper, the proposed conjecture is thoroughly examined by initially demonstrating that each Michal Szabados-periodic configuration contains specific non-expanding lines. Furthermore, it is shown under a different condition that there are specific non-expanding lines with the maximum possible length. Researchers have found a way to determine configurations that satisfy Szabados's criteria but violate Chvátal-Simon's and Quilliot's conclusions, indicating the conditions are distinct. A study found configurations that satisfy Chvátal-Simon and Quilliot's criteria, however, do not meet Michal Szabados's criteria, indicating the conditions are distinct. Lastly, it is observed that finding the shortest non-expanding lines is a problem classified as NP-complete.

In modern applications, systems modeling often involves processing high-dimensional data over time with incomplete information. Our study focuses on estimating the latent state space dynamics of time-series data, where only partial observations are available. We utilize observation projection-based dynamic mode decomposition to approximate the latent system, and establish conditions for DPDM to converge towards the underlying latent system, even with noisy and incomplete data. Our theoretical analysis provides significant room for further optimization of the method. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of DPDM in handling real-world data with missing values and noise, and its effectiveness is further demonstrated through a case study of a robot's locomotion data.

The vast amount of chess games played over the centuries has led to an enormous database of opening moves, made accessible through the Chessgames.com website, which provides network visualizations of opening strategies called relatedness networks. These visualizations, specifically for Spanish Opening strategies, have been analyzed using different algorithms to optimize navigation within the network. Our research focuses on determining the shortest paths between nodes within the network, which are then displayed using a dendrogram visualization to facilitate optimal strategy selection. By examining frequency and repertoire of games leading to each strategy, our findings enable players and coaches to select the most effective opening strategies, ultimately allowing for real-time suggestions to improve player decisions during games.

This research explores the observational characteristics of millisecond pulsars in terms of their magnetic fields, rotational periods, and masses. Our analysis is grounded in the concept of accretion-induced collapse of white dwarfs within binary star systems, enabling a more nuanced comprehension of millisecond pulsar demographics.
