The EuS/InAs heterojunction exhibits unique electronic properties at the interface. Using a theoretical model based on density functional theory calculations, researchers investigated the alignment of the conduction and valence bands in EuS and InAs. The study revealed that the conduction band maximums of both materials match at the EuS/InAs interface, while the valence band maximum in EuS is 1.1 eV lower than that in InAs. The difference in valence band positions is influenced by the type of bonding configuration, with four possible bonding patterns observed. The valence band maximum position also varies based on whether it faces a spin-up or spin-down electron, indicating a valence band offset of 0.55 eV for spin-up electrons and 1.65 eV for spin-down electrons. The researchers found that all calculated band alignments are stable under strain conditions.

A comprehensive classification system for subsets of Baire space, categorized by Borel Wadge classes, has been introduced with enhanced effectiveness. Based on Montalbán's true stage construction using ordinal notations, this framework efficiently represents not only the original stages but also more complex subsets represented by higher-order stages within the same ordinal, thus expanding upon the original method.

The recent surge in the popularity of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) has been hindered by the computational limitations of training them, a problem our solution, ClickTrain, seeks to address. Developed as a distributed training framework for neural networks on GPU clusters, ClickTrain leverages novel loss compression techniques to effectively scale out gradient information, enabling efficient training of large networks across multiple nodes. Our extensive experiments demonstrate ClickTrain's exceptional performance, achieving a remarkable 40x reduction in the training time required to reach the same accuracy as the industry standard method, BLSA, across multiple government datasets, including Cifar10, Cifar100, and LSUN.

This research examines the properties of specific mathematical structures, specifically ordered structures that combine distributivity and residual properties. We demonstrate that a broader class of matrices includes bounded distributive lattices and we obtain a new standard representation for this broader class by a method involving an inclusion of certain matrices. We establish a method to extend certain properties of these matrices. Additionally, our research shows the existence of a unique way to complete a discrete matrix to a more comprehensive matrix that includes all possible extensions. Moreover, our research provides a way to express the maximal expansion of distributive matrices in terms of non-associative, completely distributive matrices, which includes a description of the maximal associated matrix using functors. Finally, our research provides an example of a non-distributive matrix that can be maximally extended to a distributive matrix.

The convergence of gravitational wave and electromagnetic observatories will enable us to identify and analyze three distinct types of compact binary mergers - binary neutron star (BNS) mergers, neutron star (NS) - black hole (BH) mergers, and BH-BH (BH-BH) mergers - each with unique signatures.  We developed an advanced binary waveform builder called DynBurst, which seamlessly combines electromagnetic and gravitational wave signatures by generating complex binary waveform templates and corresponding electromagnetic signatures.  These sophisticated simulations will aid researchers in distinguishing BNS and NS-BH mergers from BH-BH mergers and predicting observable electromagnetic signatures.  We conducted a series of tests using DynBurst to simulate a BNS merger and simulated electromagnetic signatures within the V407 Sh2-SgrA* electromagnetic spectrum, which yielded promising results.  The model successfully reproduced the observed spectrum and predicted a range of signatures, including radio, X-ray, and gamma-ray emissions.

A new discovery has been made regarding a gas giant exoplanet, which orbits around a star significantly larger than the sun in a relatively close orbit of just 0.075 astronomical units. This exoplanet, which has been named HD 156622 b, shares similarities with another known exoplanet, Jupiter, particularly in terms of its potential primordial origin. Research suggests that had HD 156622 b maintained its current orbit over time, tidal forces would have caused it to spiral into its host star. This unique circumstance makes it an ideal candidate for studying how planets evolve and form.

A single agent decision-making problem under uncertainty, known as a constrained Markov decision process, is an operations research model that accounts for operational and performance restrictions. Researchers have developed methods to find optimal solutions, but these approaches don't scale well for larger problems, prompting a need for more efficient techniques. We propose an innovative solution, an approximate dynamic programming method, that overcomes this challenge, allowing for a practical solution to these complex problems with multiple constraints. We validate our method on two operations research models, a robust production planning problem and a collaborative logistics problem, demonstrating its effectiveness in handling constraints that are often overlooked.

In recent years, there has been a notable surge in the application of hand-written mathematical symbol recognition and generation technologies, primarily due to its significant implications in both education and research. A significant challenge in the Handwritten Mathematical Symbol Recognition and Generation (HMSR) domain is the effective and precise segmentation of complex handwritten mathematical symbols. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel framework for the effective segmentation of complex handwritten mathematical symbols. Our proposed framework leverages modern hand-written script image analysis techniques, incorporating both modern and traditional features derived from geometric shapes and textural characteristics. Furthermore, we conduct an in-depth performance evaluation of the framework using multiple datasets, showcasing its superiority over conventional methods.

A proposed method to establish a correspondence between BPS states in superconformal quantum mechanics and twisted Dolbeault cohomology classes on a resolved space is proposed. This proposed method relies on a proposed equivalence to another method to count BPS states which involves integrating over moduli spaces of sheaves. This new method of counting can be applied to situations where traditional integrals are difficult to evaluate, such as when sheaves have infinite-dimensional cohomology groups. The proposed method is tested and verified on the resolved spaces of conical singularities of A-type and D/E/F-type, and is found to yield accurate results that match existing integrals. Additionally, a new integration formula based on this method is derived and found to closely resemble known computations.

We've developed a advanced framework to examine how the structure of homogeneous and heterogeneous networks, whether network-free, impacts the prevalence of contagions like epidemics and misinformation. This framework can be applied to models that were previously used to understand contagion spread, such as the Susceptible-Infected-Susceptible model. Notably, our research reveals that in heterogeneous networks, the presence of high-degree nodes can lead to an infinite prevalence of contagions, even below the threshold required for infinite outbreaks in homogeneous networks. To address this phenomenon, we've created a new theoretical model, the Threshold Model for Network-Free systems, which accurately predicts the critical threshold for these events. This model is further generalized into the Threshold Model for heterogeneous networks, which we have found to outperform established models like the Susceptible-Infected-Susceptible models in accurately describing contagion spread.

Actor-critic reinforcement learning techniques have proven effective in generating nearly optimal actions, yet have shown limited success in early stages of training due to unreliable policy gradients. To address this challenge, we introduce the integration of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, a powerful sampling technique, into actor-critic methods, allowing for a more reliable exploration of high-reward actions even when the critic is unreliable. This addition has several advantages, including accelerating early policy updates, enhancing the reliability of this update, and improving an agent's performance in several benchmark scenarios, including those with a dynamic environment, delayed rewards, and complex mapping between observations and rewards.

It's common knowledge that any prime number greater than or equal to 5 can be represented in the form $12k \pm 1$. In this paper, we will explore the unique representation of odd integers that are products of prime numbers greater than or equal to 5, and prove that these integers can be written as either $7k \pm 1$ or $5k \mp 2$. The challenge is to find all positive integers $g, h, r$ that satisfy the equation $g(7r-1) \pm h(7r+1) \pm 2h = 1$, with $g, h \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$. In addition, we will examine a conjecture related to this equation, specifically that the only solution where $g=3$ occurs under the condition that a certain prime dividing $h$ leaves a remainder of 3 when divided by 4. If this conjecture is proven true, the set of all positive integers $r$ that satisfy the given equation with $g=3$ and $g(7r-1) \pm h(7r+1) \pm 2h = 1$ where $g, h \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$, is equivalent to the set of all positive integers $r$ that satisfy the equation with $g=3$ and

Autonomous navigation in diverse and complex environments poses significant challenges for sensor performance, particularly when sensor modalities experience performance degradation due to adverse weather conditions. This issue is particularly pronounced when navigating through rain or snow. To navigate effectively in such scenarios, robots must be capable of adapting to modified sensor data, which may not align with the conditions the robot was designed for. To address this problem, researchers have developed an approach that enables robots to navigate through rainy and snowy conditions using only typical sensor data. This approach involves learning a mapping between rain/snow and clear weather images, transforming the rain/snow images into clear views. The true view, however, cannot be directly confirmed without real-world robot interactions. Therefore, researchers have developed a self-supervised learning approach that combines image translation with generative world models to identify inconsistencies in the translated images. The method is validated through extensive experiments on various datasets, including outdoor scenes, satellite imagery, and synthetic data.

The origins of flat spectra in space objects have long been debated, with various theories proposed including complex carbohydrates, polymers, and minerals such as olivine and pyroxene. In our study, we analyzed the spectral characteristics of the dwarf planet Ceres using CERES, a spectral instrument on a cycler spacecraft. Ceres shows evidence of water ice on its surface, as well as features indicative of recent activity, such as bright spots and plumes. Ceres is composed of a mixture of various materials, including olivine and pyroxene minerals, which we used to model the instrument's response. By comparing our model to the observed spectral data, we found a significant discrepancy between the two datasets, particularly at shorter wavelengths. To resolve this mismatch, we found that a constituent with a neutral spectrum, resembling C, O, H$_2$, N, and N$_2$ compounds, could potentially explain the observed spectral features on Ceres. This neutral-sloped material may be present on the surface of Ceres and other space objects, including the Moon and asteroids.

Let $\mathcal{R}_n(q)$ be the ring of lower triangular matrices of size $n \times n$ over the finite field $\mathbb{F}_{\mathcal{Q}(q)}$. This study investigates the unique finite structure $\mathfrak{S}_{n,\mathcal{Q}}((\mathbb{F}_{\mathcal{Q}})_{n \times n}))$, formed by non-free cyclic right $\mathfrak{R}_n(q)$-modules with elements from the injective module $\mathbb{I}(\mathfrak{R}_n(q))$. It is demonstrated that this unique structure is isomorphic to an $(\mathbb{F}_{\mathcal{Q}})_{(q^{(n \choose 2)})}$ and comprises $q^{(n \choose 2)}$ points with $\binom{q^{(n \choose 2)}-1}{q-1}+\cdots+\binom{q-1}{q-1}$ lines. Additionally, it is shown that the underlying graph $\underline{\mathfrak{S}_{n, \mathcal{Q}}}((\mathbb{F}_{\mathcal{Q}})_{n \times n}))$ of the finite structure has a connected, strongly $\mathfrak{t}$-kaylaxian, and rayer property, with $\chi(\underline{\math

In a 1984 paper in J. Symbolic Logic, Pawlikowski demonstrated that under specific conditions, certain types of real numbers almost certainly exist within certain mathematical models. Specifically, he found models containing only one type of real number, known as a Cohen real, when considering either random or Cohen real scenarios. This article provides two methods for constructing such models, with one method relying on an existing mathematical theorem by Palyutin, Palyutin and Todorčević from 2011 in the Journal of the American Mathematical Society. Additionally, two new models were discovered that follow similar patterns, with specific rules regarding the presence of certain types of real numbers, such as those defined by Galvin and Miller in 1977.

A key aspect in creating effective long-term decision-making strategies for scenarios with uncertain outcomes involves utilizing data-driven models known as sequential decision support systems, specifically dynamic treatment regimes. The first phase of developing these regimes typically involves using observational data through a process called optimistic reduction. By eliminating sub-optimal actions based on the pessimism principle, this initial reduction enhances the reliability of the subsequent model's input. In order to address issues of data distribution and parameter changes, our study incorporates a novel Bayesian learning algorithm using Thompson sampling to ensure robust performance. The proposed algorithm has been successfully tested on high-dimensional data from the COBRE project using simulated inputs.

Dualities between subcategories of finitely generated modules over Artin algebras can be defined by the relationship of their Ext-orbits. Specifically, when one duality exists, the relationship of its inverse provides a corresponding duality, but this generally does not hold. We identify sufficient conditions under which this exception does not apply, leveraging properties of tilting and co-tilting modules in our analysis.

A proposed Witting configuration, with a different complexity of 40 rays, is illustrated as an intricate pattern on a 12-dimensional sphere, linked to a Dehn twist in this configuration. The arrangement is visualised through great circle connections, aligning with the geometric foundations underpinning C. H. T. Dowker's research on the Dehn twist. This setup offers a novel demonstration of the proposed universal mechanism driving the progression of the Pascal triangle.

A theoretical model is developed in the paper to study a flat band superconductor on a honeycomb lattice within the strong correlation regime. It's demonstrated that the strongly bound pairs of electrons can move within the plane, whereas unpaired electrons remain stationary. The model naturally exhibits the Fermi surface locking phenomenon and its critical temperature is found to be in the range of 100K to 1000K, based on the parameters of the model. The results show that the theoretically predicted behavior is consistent with the observed properties of magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene.

The Gaussian distribution is uniquely determined by the distribution of a linear combination and a power function of independent identically distributed random variables. We identify the a-adic solenoids for which this relationship holds, effectively proving a theorem analogous to the generalized Polya theorem. This proof relies on solving a functional equation for a specific class of functions associated with the character group of the a-adic solenoid.

Ecological research relies heavily on statistical models, but the data collected from field studies often presents challenges in form.  Ecologists' pattern-oriented models utilize theoretical models, such as agent-based models, to inform data collection efforts and inform research priorities.  Model simulations can forecast areas where data collection is crucial and inform the design of surveys.  Despite these benefits, the large volume of ecological data and complexity of simulations pose obstacles to integrating these models into the workflow of ecologists.  To address these challenges, we introduce EcoWorkflows - a platform that integrates R functions, Excel spreadsheets, JavaScript, and Python to facilitate eco-friendly data analysis and model-based decision-making.  This platform includes features such as web interfaces, interactive visualizations, and interactive dashboards to enable ecologists to visualize and interpret their data and model results.  By providing modular tools and promoting collaboration, EcoWorkflows empowers ecologists to explore novel research questions and foster knowledge-sharing within the community.

In recent years, salient object detection using deep neural networks has gained significant attention, but most current methods rely on domain-specific networks or require complex hand-crafted features. To address these limitations, we propose a novel end-to-end salient object detection framework named CEPCNet, which integrates a novel context extraction technique called cross-attention. By incorporating this mechanism, our framework can effectively capture contextual information from both spatial and color dimensions through the integration of a U-Net backbone, a fully connected CRF post-processor, and a fully connected CRF loss. The cross-attention context extraction module allows our framework to adapt to various datasets, including diverse unsupervised images, making it a versatile and adaptable solution. Extensive experiments on seven datasets demonstrate the superiority of our framework over current state-of-the-art salient object detection methods.

The UM-IU@LING system for the 2019 SemEval OffensEval Task won second place in the macro F1 score category by detecting hate speech in tweets. The team that developed this system utilized a BERT classifier which was fine-tuned using a dataset of approximately 5000 annotated tweets. They also tested different model configurations and found that using both fine-tuned BERT and a classifier with features from the text and the model's output resulted in the best performance.

A number, N, is termed a palindrome if its binary form is symmetrical. For instance, 5 in binary is represented as 101, making it a palindrome. Our research involves investigating the likelihood that the product of the numbers N and N+1 in binary form is a palindrome. This study will demonstrate that the probability of this occurrence approaches zero as the leading numbers N increases. Additionally, a computer simulation was conducted to verify this hypothesis for the initial 10 million positive integers N.

Computed tomography (CT) is increasingly utilized in various fields such as industrial, environmental, and security scanning systems that utilize broad energy X-ray beams. However, such beams can introduce image distortions like energy-dependent beam attenuation, hardening, and streaking. To address these challenges, researchers are exploring multi-energy CT techniques that reconstruct material maps based on energy-specific attenuation coefficients. This paper proposes an analytical approach to estimating the polyenergetic beam hardening effect, enabling the development of a globally convergent algorithm to correct this artifact. The method demonstrates global convergence due to its incorporation of a non-symmetric forward-backward splitting framework, with simulations showing its effectiveness in mitigating artefacts and outperforming an existing artefact correction method.

Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) has seen significant advancements thanks to Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs). However, these technologies still face limitations in resources-constrained contexts, such as when dealing with historical documents or documents with limited training samples. One area where CNNs and RNNs can be improved is in how they handle training data. A new approach, known as the Hybrid Transformer-CNN-RNN model, combines the strengths of these technologies with new techniques like Transformer models, self-attention, and attention-based RNNs. The Hybrid Transformer-CNN-RNN model outperforms existing methods on challenging tasks, including recognition of Low-Resolution documents and Low Resource settings.

We have developed a novel, non-iterative method to determine the upper energy limit beyond which an many-body calculation becomes meaningless due to its sensitivity to unknown high-momentum interactions. This method was tested in numerous ab initio calculations performed with the similarity renormalization group approach, focusing on nuclei near the $^{16}$O core, involving up to 10 particle holes. By comparing our predictions with actual estimates of the high-momentum distribution, we found that our method yields conservative results, making nearly all computed states physically reliable. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the most demanding calculations can still be accurately computed up to approximately 6 times the momentum where the high-momentum distribution significantly drops, allowing for nearly complete high-momentum distributions to be calculated with enough accuracy for most practical purposes.

We invite undergraduate students to explore the fascinating world of one-dimensional topological phases, focusing on the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. By understanding basic linear algebra and quantum mechanics, students can grasp key concepts such as wavefunction localization, robustness, and the significance of Hamiltonian symmetry. Through calculation of exact eigenstates and the use of the Zak phase, students can find analytical expressions for eigenenergies, eigenstates, and phase values for small systems. Additionally, for larger systems, students can leverage pseudomode techniques and the concept of winding numbers to explore robust topological edge modes in the context of experimental measurements.

This study examines the compactness of composition operators within Bergman spaces associated with certain bounded, convex domains in complex n-dimensional space containing non-trivial analytic circles in the boundary. This finding confirms previous results for the Bergman space of unit ball and provides a new characterization of compactness for these spaces.

We derived a two-loop amplitude formula for the s-channel, obtaining the amplituhedron as a direct consequence. Furthermore, it has been discovered that this two-loop amplitude can be expressed in terms of a geometric object constructed from a product of two adjacent AdS spaces, effectively eliminating spurious poles through the application of a holographic renormalization process, and thus rendering the result finite. The approach to resolving such singularities offers an intriguing new strategy for understanding and resolving such issues. Notably, this method also provides a more intuitive explanation of the Eikonal limit, and it has been provided an explicit check that this approach yields the correct Eikonal expression. The approach to resolving such singularities has the potential to be applied to other scenarios, including massless external states.

High-performance computing has witnessed significant growth in the last two decades, driving a growing interest in exploring the applications of shared-memory parallel programming techniques. This paper contributes to this exploration by introducing Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO) paradigm as a unified framework for implementing shared-memory parallelism. Research in SMMO focuses on investigating its feasibility through the implementation of a C extension, named SCC ext, as well as a standalone SCC sh compiler. The proposed solutions are then applied to a variety of computational problems involving multiple instances of the same task. Results show that SCC ext, integrated into GCC, performs comparably to task-based implementations, particularly for applications exhibiting object independence and uniform object access patterns. Additionally, SCC sh outperforms a manually parallelized version of a search algorithm by a factor of 1.72, although its advantage diminishes as object interactions become more prevalent.

We introduce family universal U(1)X models incorporating three right-handed neutrinos, which naturally accommodate the 0.4 eV lower limit set by Kosmos-2019 for dark matter. These models, consistent with lepton flavor universality violation in charged currents, feature a dark matter candidate that arises from the spontaneous breaking of a global U(1) symmetry, resulting in a non-zero ZAX coupling with neutrinos. This coupling enables dark matter detection through neutrino backgrounds in detectors like Xenon-1T and is compatible with the stated dark matter mass range.

A specific measurement technique for assessing the mechanical characteristics of straw tubes is presented, which uses the knowledge of tube wall thickness to calculate Young's modulus and other elastic properties. These characteristics are derived by measuring tubes in an air-filled environment and calculating their longitudinal vibration frequencies, along with determining the wall thickness using ultrasonic sound waves. A calculation is performed to identify the Poisson's ratio of the straw tube, using measurements of the tube when submerged in a liquid with a known density, which also allows for calculating the liquid's static modulus of rigidity. As an additional outcome of this research, a finite element model was created for predicting the natural frequencies of vibrating strings, which includes effects of the string's own weight, providing a more accurate and comprehensive analysis compared to the classical model that neglects these factors.

We investigate the maximum marginal probability problem, specifically for determining the optimal output given fixed inputs, across multiple decision functions. This is referred to as MARmax and has applications in areas like finding the best subgraph in a graph, making entry decisions in a supply chain, and multi-objective optimization. While some instances of MARmax can be resolved in polynomial time, the general problem is NP-hard. Consequently, we focus on developing approximation algorithms. Our research includes: 1) a universal lower bound approximation that is based on decision functions' marginal probabilities being lower or equal to independent probabilities; 2 an approximation that can be used when the decision function is randomized; and 3 an approximation framework for MARmax when applied to Bayesian networks.

In a supersolid Bose-Einstein condensate with a spin-orbit coupling, an accelerated impurity atom exhibits oscillations that mirror Bloch oscillations in solid matter, despite causing condensate excitements that generate the oscillations. These movements are deeply embedded in the condensed particle framework and are influenced by the condensed impurity interaction, without requiring an external gradient. The discovery is a quantum manifestation of the Einstein--de Haas effect, linking atomic motion to condensation dynamics, and could potentially be observed through impurity atom interferometry for selecting optical parameters.

In 1991, a family of code-based generalized quadrangles was first introduced by a set of parameters based on certain lengths, minimum distances and sizes. Recent studies in 2019 confirmed a conjecture made in 1991 and fully characterized quads derived from a specific type of code. Our study delves into further generalization of these quads, focusing on cases where the minimum distance is four and analyzing the structural properties of these configurations. We utilize minimal linear sets in a projective line to investigate generalized quads, particularly through a set of parameters. Our research reveals the existence of generalized quads in specific lines and utilizes this finding to establish the existence of generalized quads for specific parameters, while also utilizing this result to validate the existence of generalized quads in specific lines and utilize this discovery to establish the existence of generalized quads for specific parameters.

A new study using the JWST's MIRI instrument to observe the central region of our galaxy, the Milky Way, has revealed detailed insights into its molecular gas composition. Researchers examined the gas in this area, which extends up to 300 parsecs from the center, and found that the density of the gas is not uniform, becoming significantly more compact as one moves closer to the center. Furthermore, the observed structure of the gas appears to be influenced by the presence of massive stars in its area, with the gas being displaced in certain directions by their radiation pressure. The research also found a strong correlation between the molecular gas composition and the presence of hot dust in the central region of our galaxy.

Understanding how intense X-ray beams affect matter is a pressing issue in x-ray free-electron laser research. To investigate this effect, an experiment utilizing zinc oxide was conducted. An innovative method to analyze the data was devised, breaking down zinc's 3d and oxygen's 2p electronic states into separate components. By doing so, researchers uncovered that transitions involving 3d electrons show a steady increase in absorption, while those involving oxygen 2p electrons initially display increased absorption before eventually decreasing. Calculations based on time-dependent theory and  simulations  based  on  modified  energy  levels  showed  that  this  observed  phenomenon  could  be  explained  by  electrons  moving  to  higher  energy  levels  and  blocking  the  absorption  of  photons  for  oxygen  states  specifically.  Furthermore,  researchers  found  that  when  considering  both  zinc  and  oxygen  states,  oxygen  exhibits  increased  absorption  at  lower  fluences,  but  this  increased  absorption  eventually  decreases,  showing  a  decline  at  higher  fluences,  with  this  decrease  starting  around 10^13 photons/(cm^2 pulse).

This research presents a novel temperature sensing system incorporating a CMOS sensor, designed for integration into high-performance computing systems with the capability of adaptive voltage frequency scaling. The paper showcases the design of a high-speed temperature sensor and conditional dynamic voltage scaling controller, along with a low-power, sub-microwatt implementation achieved through 180nm technology. Key metrics for evaluating the sensor's performance are introduced, with measured results demonstrating accurate temperature readings within 1.5°C across a 30°C range and precise thresholds within 1°C, all while utilizing adaptive voltage frequency scaling to optimize power efficiency.

Quantum entanglement is a fundamental concept in quantum information science and technology, with a particular focus on polarization entanglement due to its crucial role. We have developed a new method for creating entangled states of polarization using a doped photonic crystal fiber that emits two wavelengths simultaneously, which occurs when an erbium/thulium co-doped fiber is pumped with a single light source. This method takes advantage of the erbium emission at 1545 nm and the simultaneous thulium emission at 1540 nm and 2100 nm. We demonstrate that the ratio of their powers and the degree of correlation can be controlled using a variable optical attenuator and an optical circulator, respectively. This method has shown a high degree of correlation (above 80%) and a low polarization visibility error of 3.5%, which indicates its potential for practical applications in quantum information technology.

This paper explores the concept of online Euclidean spanners in multiple dimensions. It considers the case where a sequence of points in R^d is given one at a time, and the algorithm must create and update a geometric t-spanner for each set of points as it arrives. A key finding is that for online $(1+\epsilon)$-spanners in one-dimensional space, a lower bound of $\Omega(\log_{1+\epsilon} n)$ applies, along with a lower bound of $\Omega(\log_{1+\epsilon} n / \epsilon)$ for general d-dimensional space. These lower bounds hold for specific point sequences, including complete binary trees and can be adapted to apply to general d-dimensional space. Upper bounds are considered for specific types of t-spanners, including strict and relaxed variants, with significant improvements proposed for certain conditions. Notably, an upper bound of $O(t^{2d} \log_{1+\epsilon} n)$ is given, along with techniques to reduce this bound under certain conditions where the angle between dimension axes is less than or equal to $d$. It is conjectured that the upper bound could be improved such that it would not depend on $t$.

This study proposes a novel method to assign labels to various IoT devices using alternative features in place of traffic fingerprints, utilizing machine learning techniques in a two-step process. The initial phase involves selecting a distinct set of more easily extractable features from a original set of harder-to-obtain features, through the use of linear programming. This optimization also minimizes the cost associated with extracting features, given that each device has an associated extraction cost. The outcome is the selection of features that maintain high classification accuracy while minimizing extraction costs. The extracted features are then used to train a machine learning classifier for the purpose of determining device labels. The effectiveness of this approach was validated using the UMD17 dataset, in comparison with a traditional fingerprinting-based classifier and a classifier using all available features, revealing that this method dramatically reduces feature extraction costs with little to no performance decline, thus significantly enhancing the efficiency of unsupervised device learning.

Godel modal logics can be regarded as an intermediate Godel-C2jC progression between the basic intuitionistic modal logic and its stronger constructivizations, which are characterized by a broader spectrum of semantic frameworks, including semantics based on finite, bounded, and algebraic structures. In this context, a comprehensive investigation is conducted to provide sound and complete axiomatizations for Gentzen-style sequent calculi and Tarski-style Hilbert systems. Additionally, these logics' relationships with fundamental closure operators and their corresponding algebraic semantics are thoroughly explored.

This paper presents a novel and straightforward technique for word-alignment that leverages bilingual information from external sources like machine translation platforms. We demonstrate that a model with limited parameters can achieve performance comparable to GIZA++ when trained on a relatively small dataset. Furthermore, in cases of training with a mininal dataset, our proposed method surpasses it by notable margins.

We suggest an asynchronous algorithm to solve Nash equilibrium problems by iteratively decomposing the mixed strategies. This methodology is heavily grounded in monotone operator theory, utilizing warped resolvents for handling a combination of nonsmooth and smooth functions involved in strategy mixtures.

The concept of primordial black holes (PBHs) has been proposed as a possible explanation for dark matter. It's theorized that these black holes could form during the early stages of the universe's development. Our model examines the generation of PBHs that could potentially be created by cosmic string loops collapsing. We've discovered that PBHs can be formed when certain conditions are met, specifically when the shape of the black hole's mass distribution matches that of the cosmic string loop. As a result, primordial black holes may serve as detectors for cosmic gravity waves emanating from cosmic gravity waves.

We investigated how particles behave in computer-simulated models of uniform, wedge-shaped molecules. These molecules' shapes are defined by a single parameter that controls how pointed they are. Our models accounted for different levels of density and used various types of boundary conditions to observe the phases the systems went through. For low-density systems, we observed a nematic phase in two dimensions and reported nematic and smectic A phases in 3D. For high-density systems, we observed complex liquid crystalline phases and noted that for very round molecules, the systems displayed a face-centered cubic packing pattern. For very polar molecules, the systems displayed a body-centered tetragonal packing pattern. We also observed a body-centered tetragonal phase that was stabilized by a free energy analysis.

Recurrence relations exist that connect any two successive orders of Gegenbauer polynomials. These relations allow us to determine whether a zonal function on the sphere has a purely positive Gegenbauer series expansion. By leveraging this property, we can establish connections between positive definite functions and strictly monotone functions in the context of the sphere. This relationship provides insights into the characteristics of positive definite functions on the sphere and their applications to random and directed geometric models, such as the Gaussian random field. Additionally, we derive bounded variation formulas for certain classes of spherical functions and explore extensions of theorems related to the Bochner minimum principle and Matheron's criterion for stationary random fields.

A conventional imaging setup is comprised of three key elements: a light source, the object to be imaged, and the imaging system, all operating within a confined space.  Traditional imaging systems are largely limited to two-dimensional imaging, yet imaging within confined spaces can lead to significant imaging compression.  In an effort to expand imaging possibilities into three dimensions, we have designed a compact, cost-effective LED 3D imaging system utilizing a global shutter CMOS image sensor, which is capable of reconstructing volume information from acquired two-dimensional images.  In an experiment employing this system, we successfully measured the movement of gel beads within 1 mm$^3$ and observed changes in the gel's pore structure under compression of up to 50%.  Our results demonstrate the potential for similar small-scale 3D imaging systems, opening up the possibility for extensive applications.

The flow characteristics of complex liquids in shearing motion alongside rough surfaces are studied in this research, and the results are shown to be influenced by the liquid and surface properties in a dependent manner. Through a thorough examination, the shearing motion is divided into three distinct friction regimes and a transition between them is quantified, and this analysis is supported by both theoretical modeling and experimental data. Furthermore, an existing model is tested and, in certain circumstances, requires adjustment to accurately reflect the shearing motion. This revised model is then integrated into an established framework for predicting lubrication in rough surfaces.

This report details our approach to the 2019 ISIC challenge, specifically for classifying skin cancer from dermatology images, and achieved top-tier performance by securing 1st place in 2 out of 4 tasks, 2nd place in 1 more, and 6th place in another, according to the area under the curve metric.

We carried out a high-resolution ARPES study on sodium, utilizing an excellent material quality and interface with nearly no surface contamination, to investigate the characteristics of the conduction band in sodium. Our study revealed that the band is significantly broadened due to its short lifetime. We demonstrated that existing theoretical models are insufficient to fully account for this phenomenon, and proposed that further research should focus on models that incorporate many-body interactions beyond the quasi-particle level.

Building on a novel theory, microstate nonequilibrium thermodynamics, we've successfully applied it to examine the dynamics of an ideal gas within a system experiencing free expansion. Our research delves into the behavior of this phenomenon across various time frames, from immediate to prolonged periods, and within both quantum and stochastic frameworks. As a result, we've discovered that a significant amount of work can be extracted, particularly during free expansion, and that it's performed at specific, distinct rates. Furthermore, we've found that the work done on the system adheres to the following inequalities: $\delta W_{\text{sign}}\ge 0$ in equilibrium and $\delta W_{\text{sign}}\le 0$ during free expansion. Our findings also reveal that the extracted work cannot surpass the energy released, contrary to traditional thermodynamic expectations, and we believe this process could have far-reaching implications for both thermodynamics and the design of micro-machines.

This passage provides an in-depth, explicit calculation for the weights of Kontsevich graphs that emerge from connections and curvatures within symplectic manifolds, employing an algebraic approach that can potentially be applied to other structures, such as holomorphic connections and their associated holomorphic curvains. Notably, this method reveals a simplified expression for the weights of curvature graphs, which can be expressed through group homomorphisms. However, it's essential to acknowledge that this specific approach may not extend to general connections and their curvains.

In our research, we've expanded upon previous findings related to the emergence of nanoptera in singularly perturbed Hertzian chains, particularly focusing on compacton solutions. By integrating discrete models with continuum approximations, we discovered that cross-diffusion leads to the exponential localization of waves, resulting in the exponential decay of wave tails. Chain asymmetry determines the decay rate, which implies a limited range of parameters that support nanoptera. Additionally, we've verified our hypothesis that nanoptera may exist in other compacton families, such as trigonometric family waves.

This study explores the feasibility of inflationary models based on classical oscillations, which were previously dismissed due to their inherent instability to perturbations. Our findings demonstrate that such models can indeed satisfy key criteria for successful inflation when considering certain types of classical and quantum fluctuations, particularly in the context of the early universe. This may offer a viable explanation for the observed spectrum of gravitational waves detected by future detectors, which could be consistent with the onset of a phase of oscillatory inflation.

Consider a graph $G$ with an even number of vertices, where an edge coloring partitions the edges into pairs connected by the same color. A graph has the Pairing-Hamiltonian property (PH-property) if, for every possible way of coloring its edges with one color, there's at least one Hamiltonian path in the graph that follows this coloring. In this context, it is established that complete graphs with vertices in certain configurations have the PH-property, specifically when vertices are arranged in a grid with one or more dimensions having even values. Conversely, graphs with vertices in certain odd configurations do not have the PH-property, leading to a new result confirming a previous conjecture for specific cases.

The quantum walk model has become a popular choice for simulating and studying non-equilibrium processes on various quantum devices, including trapped ion systems and photonic circuits. This paper investigates how adding coin bias and a mixing angle in the three-state quantum walk model impacts the dynamics of wavepacket spreading. Numerical simulations reveal that introducing coin bias results in the emergence of a plateau region, restricting wavepacket expansion. Conversely, adjusting the mixing angle has similar effects, but also causes the wavepacket to reverse its direction of spreading. These findings demonstrate how modifying initial conditions can significantly alter quantum transport properties, which is crucial for developing quantum sensing and communication technologies.

This paper IntiTransformer is a self-supervised Vision Transformer approach that enhances the efficiency of semantic segmentation tasks. IntiTransformer is uniquely suited for this task as it can be easily modified to account for spatial variability. Our tests show that IntiTransformer achieves superior results compared to other supervised and self-supervised learning models, such as ConvNet and Student-ViT. IntiTransformer is available for download on our repository at https://intitransformer.github.io/.

A unified dark fluid model has been developed to explain both dark matter and dark energy. It comprises a non-relativistic, undissipative component, and a dissipative fluid with an equation of state that links pressure to density. By applying the field equations of modified f(R,T) gravity, the model has been examined using thermodynamic stability principles. Stability analysis for both linear and non-linear perturbations has been conducted within the context of the model. Key parameters, such as the squared speed of sound and Cauchy index, have been determined to assess the stability of the model, particularly in relation to its transition between phantom and non-phantom phases. By utilizing numerical simulations, it was found that dissipation enhances the stability of the model, and that it remains stable beyond the transition point.

We present a straightforward proof that in three or more dimensions, the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Euler equations has a critical issue in terms of stability, specifically when using Sobolev spaces and certain types of Lorentz spaces, thereby confirming an earlier study by Bourgain and Li.

Recent advances in diffusion models have led to significant progress in image editing and generation. However, existing methods heavily rely on semantic segmentation, resulting in a decline in efficiency and the need for substantial memory resources. We present an innovative approach known as Semantic Guidance (SEGA), a system that automatically extracts semantic information from within the image and uses this to control the attention within a conditional adversarial generative adversarial network. This enables the use of large conditional images without incurring performance or quality losses. We demonstrate SEGA's effectiveness in the low-memory setting by training a conditional adversarial generative adversarial network on a resource-constrained Apple M1 laptop with limited memory and a basic CPU. This allows the model to generate images and edit them with high efficiency, using much smaller amounts of memory compared to previous models. We test SEGA's capabilities on a small laptop with limited resources and demonstrate its effectiveness in image segmentation and image editing tasks.

Recent advancements in deep learning have led to a surge in interest in addressing the reliability and transparency of these models. A significant challenge lies in addressing the uncertainty inherent in these models, which is often attributed to both label noise and functional disorder. By incorporating the principles of Bayesian deep learning, these two types of uncertainty can be effectively analyzed and understood. This approach has led to the development of a new framework, called the Entropy-Gated Neural Network, which is capable of separating the effects of noise on training data from the functional disorder in complex systems. By training this model on an ensemble of datasets, it is possible to improve the accuracy of predictions and functional understanding, which has been demonstrated through successful applications to functional magnetic resonance imaging data analysis.

Our research explores the possibility of $J/\psi$ decaying into undetected particles and proposes that this decay could be a sign of either light sterile neutrinos or the lightest supersymmetric particle. By applying constraints from $J/\psi$ branching ratio measurements that involve hadronic decays, along with considerations of supersymmetric production in $pp$ collisions at the LHC, we determine the maximum probabilities for both the neutral and charged sectors of supersymmetric particles being composed of a $J/\psi$. With the $J/\psi$ production cross-section at the LHC being significantly greater than that of $J/\psi$ production at $e^+e^-$ colliders, our analysis suggests that existing limits on $J/\psi$'s invisible decay may be evaded. Additionally, we project that future searches for $J/\psi$ disappearance at the LHC, coupled with upcoming searches for supersymmetric particles at the LHC, could offer definitive evidence for $J/\psi$'s invisible decay.

High-resolution observations of the solar photosphere are conducted using the DSTA Solar Telescope at the Guoquan Station in Tibet. The study focuses on analyzing magnetic bright points (MBPs) in a detailed time-lapse sequence. The analysis involves examining their spatial and physical properties through specific metrics and their movement over time. The key findings include: (1) MBPs conform to a log-normal distribution in terms of size and diameter. (2) Their areal coverage and diameter remain relatively stable across varying sizes. (3) Most MBPs exhibit little to no change in the least-squares and show an average decrease of about 10% in diameter over the observation period. The ongoing analysis and interpretation of these results are crucial for understanding the behavior of magnetic bright points in the solar photosphere.

Human vision can distinguish objects and actions using spatial or temporal data, but integrating these aspects, like in video, is more effective. However, current deep learning models for visual recognition, which handle high-dimensional inputs, assume time is a hidden variable, time-agnostic approach, when time should be considered explicit and meaningful, time-aware. This work focuses on time-aware visual recognition, where the aim is to extract meaningful time segments from inputs, whether they be 2D images, spatially arranged dot patterns, or 3D volumes, and use them to enhance recognition performance, which was tested through a hierarchical VGG architecture-based method, achieving notable improvements, especially in action recognition tasks, where significant improvements were found compared to existing image and volume recognition models, especially when dealing with challenging temporal cues such as those with time gaps, variations in visual elements, and differing durations.

The rapidly evolving atmosphere poses a significant challenge in weather forecasting due to its complex nonlinear dynamics. To overcome this challenge, we propose an innovative approach that leverages video transformation techniques. Our model, video Swin-Transformer, utilizes temporal context information from atmospheric data to accurately predict atmospheric variables. We enhance the effectiveness of the video Swin-Transformer by incorporating an interdependent variable connection module, which captures the relationships between different atmospheric variables. Through extensive experimentation on high-resolution atmospheric data, the proposed model achieved impressive results, surpassing existing cutting-edge methods. Notably, it demonstrated exceptional generalization capabilities on diverse datasets, particularly in predicting future atmospheric variables and establishing causal relationships between variables.

In models that expand on the $SU(2)_L \otimes SU(2)_R$ electroweak framework, a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry could prevent certain scalar fields from acquiring vacuum expectation values, resulting in viable dark matter candidates. This paper investigates the possibility of inert dark matter consisting of isoscalar fermions that interact with standard model particles through the coupling with $\mathbb{Z}_2$-odd fermionic and scalar multiplets, while also considering their connection to neutrino mass generation via the seesaw mechanism. By analyzing the one-loop corrections to $h\to \gamma\gamma$ and considering the possibility of $h$ decaying into two gamma rays and a pair of dark matter candidates, we find that the predicted rates for these processes, specifically $\Gamma(h\to \gamma\gamma)$ and $\Gamma(h\to \gamma\gamma + D\bar{D})$, are consistent with observational data from the Large Hadron Collider, particularly in the context of the $125$ GeV Higgs boson discovered in the $13$ TeV data set and its role in dark matter relic abundance.

A comprehensive study on the PPT square conjecture is presented with a notable achievement: the PPT square conjecture's validity has been rigorously demonstrated for the case involving finite-dimensional space.

Incompatible with its name, intracellular transportation is essential for maintaining and functioning of mature neurons as it facilitates the delivery of critical materials and tools for cellular upkeep, allowing cells to survive for extended periods by synthesizing necessary proteins as needed. Failure in this process is associated with the progression of neurodegenerative diseases such as Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) and Huntington's (HD). To better comprehend the cellular mechanisms underlying these diseases, we present a detailed study of the dynamics of axonal transportation in neurons affected by polyglutamine toxicity, using a combination of theoretical and computational approaches. We developed a simplified model that incorporates the toxic effects on transportation machinery, molecular interactions between proteins, and the aggregation of proteins. We analyzed the stability of this system by employing non-steady state analysis, utilizing the Sufficient Standard Technique (SST) along with numerical simulations to validate our findings.

Billion-dollar losses inflicted by banking fraud across the globe make graph-based fraud detection in transactions increasingly vital. In analyzing transaction patterns, researchers utilize graphs to identify novel and complex schemes. This research aims to identify real-world transaction network patterns, specifically network motifs within a heterogenous transaction dataset. We present a method for generating genuine banking transaction networks, allowing for comparison with models of random networks. Our results reveal distinct differences, revealing multiple high-frequency motifs in actual data. These findings are applied to a collaborative platform for network motif analysis, the MAMMOTH system, which is used in collaborative investigations at the National Crime Information Center.

The process of a stellar object losing mass due to interaction with a black hole, resulting in an intense burst of electromagnetic radiation, is known as tidal stripping. Recent research into ultra-short period stars within white dwarf stars has identified a previously unknown phenomenon - an intense and persistent burst of electromagnetic radiation, which is significantly more powerful than expected from existing models. The details of this phenomenon are explored through numerical simulations of complex fluid dynamics and electromagnetic interactions between two celestial bodies, which reveal a mechanism - a process of charged particle acceleration and electromagnetic interaction - that can explain the observed radiation burst? The process of charged particle acceleration and electromagnetic interaction between the white dwarf and the black hole plays a crucial role in producing the observed burst of electromagnetic radiation, which is consistent with the observed data?
