The BBA model has proven to be an effective tool in describing the hadronic component of meson decays. By applying BBA in a global approach, researchers can obtain a comprehensive set of form factors, which are then used to analyze the rare radiative decay of the tau lepton, $\tau^{\pm}\rightarrow\tau\gamma$. The application of BBA yields a satisfactory description of this process, allowing for the calculation of its branching ratio and the identification of the relevant B parameters within a seven-parameter space. The computed form factors also facilitate the analysis of the off-shell contributions in the radiative decay of the tau lepton, $\tau^{\pm}\rightarrow\tau\gamma$, providing a more complete theoretical framework.

This paper assesses the properties of Tversky-based real-valued function spaces, specifically focusing on their completeness, countability, and the ability to represent any given compact set, for both general and symmetric Tversky ratio models. The study establishes conditions under which these models meet the requirements to be a metric space.

Recent advancements in motion deblurring techniques based on deep learning predominantly rely on synthetic blurry images for training, which are created by convolving sharp images with motion blur kernels. However, the effectiveness of these methods is compromised due to discrepancies between synthetic and real blurry images. To overcome this limitation, our proposed framework generates realistic blur images using a motion deblurting GAN and their corresponding sharp images, which are not required as inputs. The generated pairs are then used to train a regression network for the deblurting task. Our approach's unique feature is the creation of realistic blurry images, which alleviates the need to contend with the synthetic-to-real domain gap. Our results demonstrate superior performance on public datasets, validating the proposed framework's efficacy.

Hebbian theory, which explains how brain cells learn from each other, is a widely accepted model for understanding how experience shapes neural connections. This model, which allows the brain to adapt and re-wire itself in response to various stimuli, is comparable to a self-organizing system capable of adaptive learning. A novel algorithm has been developed to implement a type of adaptive learning consistent with Hebbian principles, enabling efficient knowledge acquisition and the simultaneous extraction of multiple concepts. This work demonstrates the significance of adaptive learning, which, according to Hebbian principles, enables the brain to learn from experience and modify its connections without external input, a capability now being replicated in artificial neural networks using our proposed method.

The ultrapower of any ordered set is created as a refined version of a set, using the principles of nonstandard analysis. It involves taking quotients using a special type of function. The resulting ordered set always satisfies a specific property, which we will identify. We will apply this reasoning to create a new, improved version of existing methods for solving problems in optimization theory, particularly in areas involving ordered vector spaces. Our new approach will be seen to have a formulaic connection to an existing theory, which we will explicitly demonstrate.

Scientific breakthroughs in oncology, materials science, and other fields are frequently hindered by the time-consuming process of experimenting. To accelerate the model-based prediction process, researchers developed the concept of "in silico" training by using historical experimental data. However, a single dataset may contain varying levels of information, leading to different model performances and rankings. Our approach involves creating a unified framework that can handle multiple datasets with differing structures, updating the standard Bayesian model comparison method to maintain consistency across datasets. By maintaining an integrated probability model, we ensure consistent model ranking and provide a unified approach for adjusting the Bayesian model. Notably, our method allows for dynamic updates as new data becomes available, maintaining consistency in the Bayesian model and potentially revealing previously overlooked models that could be relevant.

Hadwiger's Coloring Conjecture posits that if a graph has n chromatic classes, it must contain a complete graph with (n-1) vertices as a minor. In this context, we've demonstrated that, assuming P does not equal NP, there is a way to determine whether a graph with n vertices has a complete graph with (sqrt(n)-2) vertices as a minor in O(2^(sqrt(log n))) time. Notably, this result implies that we can identify, for certain types of graphs, whether they have a specific graph as a minor in efficient computational time. Furthermore, we have developed a P-oracle algorithm with a complexity of O(n^4 * oracle calls) that determines the existence of a specific graph as a minor in a given graph with n vertices.

This research introduces an advanced algorithm for recovering smooth graph signals, leveraging past observations and adapting to the local characteristics of unknown kernel widths.  Leveraging generalized locally linear regression and smoothness constraints, the proposed algorithm generates adaptive estimates of the kernel width at each vertex.  Further enhancement is achieved through two novel techniques for determining optimal steps and a method for detecting changes in the signal over time.  The effectiveness of the algorithm is demonstrated through rigorous theoretical analysis and performance evaluations, which confirm its ability to accurately recover smooth graph signals across diverse graphs and settings.  In comparison to existing methods, this algorithm exhibits superior performance and a significantly reduced computational burden for large-scale applications.

Theoretical investigations have been conducted to enhance the capabilities of large-scale atom interferometers through the creation of complex, entangled atomic states linked to a common reference time, known as a Tkalya state. This research demonstrates the feasibility of producing such entangled atomic patterns using a time-based method in a two-flux atomic beam configuration, and our theoretical analysis suggests that this innovative technique enables the creation of highly entangled, fault-tolerant atomic patterns. Furthermore, our findings indicate that this approach offers the potential to mitigate the effects of technical noise and boost the sensitivity of large-scale atom interferometers, despite the presence of non-ideal conditions.

The purpose of this research is to derive optimal estimates for the first Robin eigenvalue of the anisotropic $p$-Laplace operator, expressed through a relevant anisotropic capacity of its associated domain and the use of the Anisotropic Brunn-Minkowski inequality. To accomplish this, an extreme value problem needs to be solved, initially leveraging lower and upper bounds of the anisotropic $p$-capacity of a specific type of convex bodies under Minkowski addition. Furthermore, this investigation expands upon the classical Brunn-Minkowski inequality for anisotropic convex bodies using the concept of convergence by fuzzy sets.

Deep learning models, particularly graph neural networks, have gained significant attention due to their ability to process complex, interconnected data. A key component of these networks is the Graph Convolutional Neural Network (GCNN), a generalized version of traditional CNNs that can be applied to various domains. Despite its versatility, the underlying mechanism of GCNNs remains unclear, with existing explanations falling short in providing a comprehensive understanding. To address this limitation, this study aims to provide insights into the conversion of different graph convolution methods into equivalent CNNs and offers insights into the role of learning filters in GCNNs through theoretical analysis and experimental results.

A novel self-correction technique called Self-Consistency-based Dependency Correction (SCDC) has been developed to enhance neural dependency parsers by leveraging large amounts of unannotated text. SCDC effectively addresses the challenge of acquiring ample supervised data for dependency parsing by enabling models to refine unlabelled sentences based on their own predictions. Through the SCDC framework, sentences initially parsed by a trained model are further refined through analysis of corrected segments, enabling the integration of unutilised sentences into the model-optimisation process. Our SCDC approach demonstrates considerable improvements over state-of-the-art methods in the unlabelled context, yielding substantial gains across various dependency parsing datasets, including CoNLL-2012, GSD, and UD.

Theories of supersymmetric Yang-Mills with algebra so(4N) can have non-trivial, invertible-defying symmetries. By utilizing holographic duality, we can determine the branes equivalent to these symmetries, and deduce the fusion principles for the symmetries through brane dynamics.

In continuous logic, query languages are introduced that can be applied to infinite databases. The focus of this paper is on a specific type of query in graph theory, called the CFI-query. This study determines which categories of graphs allow the CFI-query to be defined using continuous first-order formulas. By incorporating concepts from topological model theory, the paper offers a new method for defining the CFI-query in certain graph categories, such as expander graphs, graphs with bounded curvature, and families of finite abelian groups, all within a continuous framework. A key component of this approach involves using two distinct metric spaces for each graph, denoted as d1 and d2, with d1 representing a natural metric and d2 being the shortest path metric based on a specified weight for edges in the graph.

In a compound known for its magnetic properties, Eu2Ir2O7 undergoes an unusual phase transition characterized by an abrupt change in magnetism, originating from the interplay of electron interactions and the arrangement of atoms within the crystal structure. By substituting Bi for Eu in Eu2Ir2O7, researchers have created (2-x)EuIrO4+(1-x)BiIrO4-x and observed that introducing Bi induces the formation of magnetic domains and causes the compound to change from a state of ordered magnetism to paramagnetism more rapidly. Magnetism measurements show that increasing Bi's concentration causes more magnetic properties to emerge, revealing tiny regions of ordered magnetism surrounded by disordered regions. Computational models based on models describing how electrons interact within materials confirm that these magnetic regions are enclosed by regions of disordered magnetism, formed due to the influence of disorder. This discovery provides valuable insight into how magnetic properties can be affected by the irregular arrangement of atoms in materials and could have implications for the development of more efficient electronic devices.

Consider a metric space denoted as $(M, d)$, and let's consider the subset of mappings from $M$ to $M^*$, where $M^*$ is another metric space, and these mappings have a specific property of being Lipschitz-free with a constant of 1. We investigate under what conditions on the characteristics of these mappings or spaces a Lipschitz-free selection can be found for given mappings, and we also explore the existence of linear Lipschitz-free selections for certain valued mappings, including those with specific properties of full level sets.

A specific type of random variable tuple, $(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$, is classified as cyclic n-tuple when its components' joint distribution remains invariant under permutation, yet changes significantly when the order of variables is shifted cyclically. Techniques like empirical data analysis and characteristic function transformations can be leveraged to detect and quantify the degree of cyclic symmetry in varible tuples, illustrated in one instance with spectral data from certain types of quasicrystals.

This research investigates the relationship between software system run-time specifications, which can be adjusted, and the resulting non-functional properties of the system, such as performance and resource consumption. Many systems allow users to modify their run-time properties via plugins or flags, but no study has analyzed the impact of these adjustments on the system's characteristics, such as performance or resource usage. To address this, we employ automated techniques to investigate the run-time configuration properties of several popular Java-based systems, focusing on the effects of configuration specialization on user experience, including the trade-offs involved. We also evaluate these effects through a user-centric lens, taking into consideration factors like ease of configuration and system compatibility. The primary contributions of this study include an in-depth analysis of the configuration landscapes of multiple Java systems, an assessment of user perspectives on configuration specialization, and an examination of the benefits and limitations of this approach in improving system efficiency and resource consumption.

Light dark matter particles, particularly those weighing less than a GeV, pose significant challenges for direct detection methods, especially when it comes to identifying particles with masses below the GeV scale. However, the incorporation of advanced machine learning techniques, specifically convolutional neural networks, has demonstrated remarkable potential in overcoming these limitations, enabling the efficient analysis of complex experimental data, such as from the XENON1T experiment. By training a CNN on simulated data, researchers have successfully achieved a remarkable direct detection signal of sub-GeV dark matter using the XENON1T experiment, without resorting to standard statistical methods.

This paper proposes a method to produce the most entangled states, including Bell's state, by using an jaynes-cummings apparatus. Initially, the system, consisting of two identical cavities, an anti-jaynes-cummings interaction is applied, resulting in the creation of the balanced superposition of one-photon states. Subsequently, a single excited atom interacts with each cavity in the same manner, leading to Rabi oscillations in the probability of detecting a single photon. When the phase difference between the two cavities is 0, a Bell's state is obtained. If the phase difference is not 0, other types of entangled states can be produced. The range of phases available offers a way to control the amount of entanglement produced.

Detecting early signs of cardiovascular issues through continuous, non-invasive heart rate variability (HRV) detection is crucial. The proposed system utilizes advanced signal processing techniques to analyze chest-attached smart fabric sensors, which are used to monitor the electrical activity of the heart. A filter combining median and moving average algorithms effectively removes motion artifacts, while a custom developed feature extraction method utilizes a time-frequency analysis approach to optimize computational efficiency. Utilizing data from over 50 individuals, including both healthy participants and those with recorded motion events, we demonstrate that our proposed HRV feature set yields superior results, outperforming traditional features in terms of processing speed and overall performance.

We analyze large deviations of power input by an active force on a particle in
equilibrium with its environment. The particle behaves like an active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck
particle, subject to Langevin dynamics. A rate function is established to describe
fluctuations in power input over long periods in both unconstrained and confined
situations. The rate function is computed explicitly, especially in the case of an
unconstrained particle, where it is proven to be equivalent to certain entropic forces.
The proof involves utilizing the Gallavotti-Averbeck variational principle and leverages
estimates of Langevin potential flow in both scenarios.

This research introduces HUMBI, a large, diverse dataset designed to enhance the understanding of human body language and its impact on communication. The dataset comprises model annotations of key body signals, such as hand positions, arm movements, posture, torso orientation, and overall body configuration, derived from real video recordings of human-subAI agent interactions. To validate the significance of these annotated body signals, we conduct initial agent simulations and find that the agent incorporating these signals exhibits comparable, sometimes even superior, performance to the agent that receives textual information from the human. This discovery underscores the substantial value of interpreting body language in agent tasks. To facilitate further investigation, the HUMBI dataset and relevant code are made publicly available at https://github.com/utau-lab/Human_Interaction_Research_Hub.

Despite the growing interest in natural language processing for lower-resource languages, there is significant unused potential in leveraging the abundance of internet text for these languages to improve neural model performance. We're interested in developing a universal approach that enables seamless model transfer from English to any other language without requiring task-specific fine-tuning. Our framework, built on the concept of framework-free learning, enables seamless model transfer across tasks and languages, with a focus on sequence labeling. By combining this approach with the recent advancements in multilingual tokenization, we enable effective knowledge transfer between languages and training from general English data alone. Our approach is demonstrated to be effective through successful transfer learning of several pre-trained models to multiple languages in diverse applications.

A well-constructed deep neural network can significantly enhance the quality of standard-definition videos, but this method is limited to processing one frame at a time, thereby neglecting temporal information, which is crucial for a natural video. To address this issue, we propose a novel end-to-end trainable VSR model, named TD2T, that integrates a recently developed approach of incorporating second-order grid propagation with a flexible flow-guided alignment technique. By integrating these components, TD2T is capable of effectively exploiting both short- and long-term motion patterns to generate high-resolution videos. Moreover, the proposed model exhibits superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art VSR models, as evidenced by our experimental results, both quantitatively and qualitatively.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can significantly benefit parameter efficiency when multiple tasks are closely related.  However, if unrelated tasks are included, this advantage is compromised due to negative transfer and learning difficulties. To overcome this challenge, we introduce a novel approach called MTRLSelfDiagnosis, which enables a learner to identify and adapt to both relevant and irrelevant tasks dynamically. By incorporating an online selection mechanism, our method can isolate useful information from less relevant tasks and adjust its shared representation accordingly, thereby improving performance across all tasks. Through thorough evaluation on a variety of environments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, which outperforms strong baselines and shows consistent improvement when irrelevant tasks are added.

We have developed a class of optimal protocols in real-time for heat engines that operate within specific boundaries. These protocols maximize efficiency when driven by scale-invariant processes and also consider the effects of homogeneous systems. Within a broad framework, we establish the nature of these protocols using mathematical assumptions and provide general formulas for their key characteristics. Furthermore, our research provides concrete examples, such as those based on the Brownian motion of a particle in potential fields or the lossless compression of information, to illustrate the broad applicability of these protocols. Notably, our research reveals that the maximum efficiency protocols often fall within the class of time-dependent changes in system parameters that were once considered as the maximum efficiency protocol in equilibrium thermodynamics.

This research proposes a probabilistic model to assess the resilience of distribution networks in the presence of combined threats from hurricanes and rising sea levels, where the primary form of damage considered is to power substation capacity resulting from sea level surges, and extended outages are caused by extended extreme weather conditions. The study utilizes a case study involving the Florida Power Corporation's grid in Fort Myers, utilizing detailed distribution system and asset data. Prescriptive measures, such as increased equipment durability, strategic repositioning, and distribution network redesign, are proposed using an iterative process in conjunction with an optimization method referred to as RC-FR.

This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space.

We define new families of parameterized piecewise affine transformations on the plane, specifically homological baker maps, which can be decomposed into two linear components with different eigenvalues for their slope matrices. These transformations exhibit heterochaos properties due to having distinct scaling behaviors in different directions. A set of parameterized families, including the generalized heterochaos baker maps, preserve a smooth invariant measure with specific singularities, and dynamic properties can be fully understood through a symbolic representation. Both typical orbits and typical transversal sections of the phase space were analyzed, with the latter matching the invariant measure. Using the Lebesgue measure for a specific one-parameter family of maps with $f(x,y)=(2kx, \frac{y}{2k})$, typical orbits and transversal measures can be measured in terms of dimension, and this can be applied to obtain estimates for the invariant measure, orbit, and transversal measure for the generalized map.

Following the groundbreaking detection of the Higgs boson in 2012, the field of particle physics has entered an exciting period. A pressing challenge for the scalar sector is now the pressing need to determine the precise properties of this particle, including whether additional scalar particles exist elsewhere in nature. By examining upcoming developments and potential breakthroughs, the authors provide a predictive outlook for the field, with the ultimate goal of guiding experimental efforts.

A new approach called the Conditional Dual-Rate Dilated Convolution Network (CDRN) is introduced, which utilizes two parallel dilated convolution layers with varying resolutions to sample and process audio signals at different rates, thereby reducing the amount of data needed for the model to learn the relationship between pitch and audio characteristics. For the condition of pitch, a neural network called the Pitch Encoding Network (PEN) is used to encode the pitch sample into a pen code, which is then used by the CDRN to generate the audio waveform. The CDRN is trained using a mixture of pen code and noise as the input, with the goal of reducing the amount of information needed from the pitch encoding network. As a result, the CDRN can be used for applications such as audio pitch detection and synthesis.

Recommender Systems based on Collaborative Filtering are effective in recommending items to users, but their performance can be hindered by the cold start and sparsity issues. To overcome this limitation, a new method called HCF-SAM was developed, which integrates both spatial and temporal information into the existing collaborative filtering framework. Specifically, hcf-SAM utilizes an inverse distance weighting system to give greater importance to the more relevant information from similar users, while also utilizing an attention mechanism to prioritize time-based similarity between users, while suppressing noise. As their names suggest, sam-SAM is derived from the statistical and adaptive samplings of the existing user behavior patterns. HCF-SAM was tested against existing state-of-the-art models, including VCF, UFMC, RecFormer, and RecFormer, using real-world datasets, and demonstrated superior performance, with improvements of up to 5.4% in prediction accuracy.

Stellar activity poses a significant challenge in identifying Earth-like planets using the Doppler technique, particularly when searching for signals weaker than the variations caused by the star's activity itself, which are referred to as the amplitudes of the "habitable planets of interest." Until recently, it was believed that the activity signals originated from the star's magnetic cycle, causing changes in features like spots, granules, and magnetic elements, all of which have activity signals significantly stronger than those of a habitable planet. However, research has recently demonstrated that star-planet signals can be detected within this framework, and the complexity of stellar activity models can be increased to account for activity signals originating from different stellar layers, thereby improving our ability to separate false positives from genuine signals, particularly when analyzing young stars, and ultimately leading to a more accurate assessment of the habitability of planets discovered through the Doppler technique.

To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana modes and those from other sources, our group is developing an interface between a majorana nanowire and an ultra-clean superconducting material. Our approach involves utilizing molecular beam epitaxy to precisely grow a thin layer of a superconducting material on the majorana nanowire, ensuring minimal disorder. By implementing this method, our laboratory has achieved the world's largest recorded Majorana peak at room temperature, as well as its rapid contraction with decreasing temperature, ultimately vanishing below 4.2 K. Our ultra-clean hybrid structures exhibit the highest recorded temperature scale for observing Majorana modes.

The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through an intuitive, higher-categorical approach, we establish a generalised THH theory for shadows and prove a comprehensive axiomatic theorem. This theorem not only confirms that shadows exhibit invariance under Morita equivalence but also reveals a distinct relationship between the shadows of a multiplicative shadow-bimodule and its traces.

Common image enhancements or edits like contrast adjustments, color changes, tone curves applications, and image blending can be ambiguous, with multiple possible outcomes for the same operation. This study introduces two distinct approaches to address this ambiguity by incorporating prior knowledge about the possible transformations. The first method utilizes paired images for training a network to predict multiple solutions by employing a probabilistic mapping between images. The second approach,PaLMAP, is paired-data-independent and is based on self-supervised learning using paired images to create an unsupervised pre-training framework for predicting multiple transformations. The experimental results show that both methods produce satisfactory outcomes when applied to real-world data. The source code for our model is freely accessible at https://github.com/ashleyg20/PaLMAP.

This technical report showcases the winning model for the TMK-2021 challenge, centered on long-video understanding. We chose to apply a simple yet effective architecture, featuring two core components. To tackle the issue of longer videos containing excessive frames that hinder performance, we implemented a temporal sampling strategy to reduce them. For the actual understanding of the down-sampled video, we employed pre-trained models like PCL and TCN as starting points and combined their outputs using a basic fusion method. Although our approach didn't achieve top accuracy for all tasks, it demonstrated strong performance in the video link prediction task and showed that even with some modifications to the architecture, significant improvements in performance were feasible.

Our simulation of snowflake dynamics in varying wind conditions reveals the significant influence of atmospheric turbulence on snowflake formation. Snowflakes, being as light as 1-2 mg, are highly sensitive to atmospheric conditions. To gain a deeper understanding of their behavior, we conducted a detailed study using numerical models and found that the atmosphere's turbulent eddies, especially those near the size of the snowflakes, cause the flake's settling speed to decrease by 20-50%. This phenomenon is essential to consider when modeling snowflake interactions with larger objects like snowballs or the accumulation of snow on power lines, as it explains, in part, why these objects often appear to have a blue tint.

This review explores the theory of active inference, a framework for understanding and modeling how living beings reduce uncertainty about what they experience and anticipate the consequences of their actions. By examining the historical development of active research, we will trace its progression from its inception within a neurobiological context to its broader applications in research fields such as cognitive science and artificial intelligence. We will also highlight the significant connections between active inference, precognitive science known as free energy minimization, and other influential concepts in our analysis.

In experimental sciences such as high energy physics and cosmology, processing real-time data streams poses significant challenges, requiring advanced techniques for online analysis. The rapid increase in data produced by these disciplines necessitates a new generation of real-time computing systems to support immediate insights from experiences. To address this need, we introduce the concept of real-time feedback modeling, a set of methods designed to simplify tasks such as detection, parameter estimation, and prediction by breaking them down into two phases: event prediction and anomaly detection. The first phase involves predicting upcoming events, and the second focuses on identifying discrepancies between predicted and actual results. This two-step process can be effectively implemented using high-performance computing systems with multiple GPUs and linear machines, demonstrating its potential on systems like the Large Hadron Collider and the Square Kilometre Array.

Utilizing Finzi's gravity theory that enhances interactions at large scales, we analyze galaxy clusters from a thermodynamic perspective, establishing a statistical model to derive thermodynamic equations and comparing clustering behavior with Newtonian gravity. We also explore the general distribution function's behavior as the clustering order increases, specifically in comparison to the standard Newtonian framework, where the distribution's peak shifts to higher densities, indicating more massive cluster formation, with a corresponding decrease in peak density relative to the standard model, as the scale increases.

A specific type of geometric hypergraph, known as convex geometric hypergraphs, can be characterized by a complete set of vertices connected to distinct edges. In this study, we examine the maximum edge count in classes of convex geometric hypergraphs that satisfy specific color constraints under multiple colors. Furthermore, we define and explore a strain variant of these groups, providing key results in this context, including all possible key values for certain constraints. Our research also highlights open problems related to these challenges.

To analyze the angular distribution of $\alpha$-particles produced in proton interactions with deuterium, we've developed a comprehensive framework for calculating the complete cross-section. This takes into account the combined effect of all relevant processes, including direct $\alpha$ production, charge exchange via the $(p,n)$ reaction with subsequent $\alpha$-decay of $^3$He through virtual states, and the sequential $pd\rightarrow^3$He$n\rightarrow\alpha$. Our calculations for the $\alpha$ angular distribution show good agreement with experimental data from KeV to MeV energy ranges, specifically with both the low-energy results from the Alpha Energy Range Interferometer and the higher-energy data from the Alpha Spectrometer, with the former being published in [Phys. Rev. C 94, 025802 (2016)] and the latter with a published update in the literature.

A previously overlooked movement technique discovered in the Pacific Lamprey sheds new light on its application to the design of climbing robots. A simulation model of the Pacific Lamprey has been developed to analyze the underlying physics of their contracting behavior. A novel robot design called Trident leverages these principles to effectively climb smooth vertical surfaces using the same movement pattern. This unique robot achieves a peak climbing speed of 1.5 cm/s and can navigate at an incline as steep as 20 degrees before slipping, outperforming other state-of-the-art climbing robots in both speed and efficiency of navigation.

This paper outlines a novel probabilistic framework designed to identify the most effective combinations of treatments in cases of colon cancer-induced immune response. An Itō stochastic process models the colon cancer dynamics, whose probabilistic evolution is governed by the Fokker-Planck equation. To identify optimal treatment combinations, an open-loop control optimization issue is proposed. Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

Optimizing wireless communication in urban and rural areas is hindered by limited infrastructure, which can be mitigated through closer proximity connections, like those in device-to-device (D2D) communication. Research has explored enhancing these connections, focusing primarily on improving energy efficiency, through various methods including routing, network layer protocols, and data encoding techniques. However, these approaches fail to fully capitalize on opportunities at the device's display level. We propose an innovative strategy to boost D2D communication performance by leveraging D2D communication opportunities at the device's display level. We introduce an optimal scheduling method based on a non-convex optimization problem that balances energy efficiency and latency, considering multiple devices, their locations, and human movement patterns. Due to its inherent complexity, we develop an approximate solution using successive convex approximation, resulting in a computationally efficient algorithm with multiple parameters. We evaluate the effectiveness of this algorithm using a combination of simulated and real-world data, taking into consideration latency and human movement patterns in urban environments.

Moffatt first discussed the concept of helicity in a fluid without viscosity in reference [25] and explored its preservation in the case of barotropic, compressible flow with smooth solutions. This paper demonstrates that weak solutions to this system in a specific mathematical space ensure the conservation of helicity. Additionally, similar results were found for both homogeneous incompressible Euler equations and the surface quasi-geostrophic equation.

The researchers in a particular study extended the solutions found in complex geometric optics to a related system of equations, which was initially investigated in contexts of electrical impedance tomography and the integrable Davey-Stewartson II equations, focusing particularly on the large spectral parameter $k$ in a specified domain $D$. They developed asymptotic solutions for the impinging and transmitted waves and used these to determine the reflection and transmission coefficients. By integrating the solutions for $u$ and $v$, the transmission eigenvalues were identified as values of $k$ for which the reflection coefficient equals zero. It was found that for certain domains $D$ and impedance parameters $\gamma$, the transmission eigenvalues exhibit transmission resonances, which were analyzed through the transmission eigenfunctions. Notably, these eigenfunctions display irregular patterns characterized by the reflection of wavefronts, which vary depending on the parameters.

Calculations for the impact of gravity waves on binary systems of compact objects, with no spin interaction, in the final stages before merging, showed that there are notable eccentricities at frequencies around 30 Hz. This was determined using an approach that involves calculating the probabilities of merging based on binary systems' eccentricities, which were then compared to predictions made using simplified models. These results indicate that the probability of merging for eccentric systems is greater than that of circular systems, particularly for certain mass ranges of the components. This finding has implications for the detection methods used by detectors like LIGO/VIRGO/KAGRA and future detectors like LIGO-A+ and KAGRA-B+, which may be able to detect certain eccentric systems up to an eccentricity of 0.1. To better understand the impact of eccentricities on the detected signals, it is suggested that new methods for analyzing these signals be developed to accurately model and remove the influence of eccentricities from the detected signals.

A technique called B\"oersch deflection or wave guide deflection has proven effective in enhancing the resonance of various systems, notably free-electron lasers (FELs). While traditional implementations rely on an electromagnetic wave, we introduce a model where a charged particle in the bunch tail deflects the storage ring wall, causing more significant deflection and potentially better efficiency improvements. In the presence of this modified model, we found that the radiation lifetime is increased by approximately two orders of magnitude, and our analysis indicates that it might yield a higher extraction rate, outperforming conventional methods.

Graph-based machine learning has gained significant attention in the past decade due to its effectiveness in modeling intricate relationships within diverse applications such as bioinformatics, chemoinformatics, and social networks. A particular area of interest is subgraph-based methods for detecting patterns in dynamic graphs, which often face issues like high false positives from noisy data and poor generalization on unseen data. To overcome these challenges, a new technique called DGLM-Det has been developed, utilizing dynamic graph machine learning for subgraph-based pattern detection. By leveraging a label correction technique derived from graph theory and incorporating self-supervised learning for unsupervised edge weighting, DGLM-Det enhances accuracy and generalization capabilities, outperforming existing state-of-the-art approaches in various real-world applications and scenarios under different evaluation metrics.

The solutions of the Guderley problem involving an imploding shock wave in an ideal gas are examined through the lens of asymptotic analysis. The accelerating shock wave's behavior is first analyzed and then its asymptotic solutions are derived, which can be expressed in terms of the self-similar exponent and logarithmic functions. Additionally, the solutions for a power-law varying background density environment are also examined.

The growing presence of artificial intelligence systems has led to a significant rise in the need for their explanations. Transparency and stakeholder trust are achieved by reducing the opacity of these systems through the provision of explanations. In this paper, we will explore the interconnection between explainable AI and requirements engineering. The challenges in the XAI field will be highlighted, along with the opportunities it presents for requirements engineers. Our primary objective is to identify potential areas where requirements engineers can make meaningful contributions to the development of transparent and trustworthy AI systems.

Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to personalize patient treatment, yet this process is labor-intensive and requires years of training for pathologists. The growing number of histology images necessitates efficient and reliable automated tools to assist in diagnosis and reduce workloads. The deep learning-based approach utilizing U-Net models has shown potential in segmenting and classifying objects within images, driving interest in applying it to medical image analysis. In this study, we evaluate the performance of deep learning models on three datasets containing adenoma, sessile Serrated and traditional Serrated polyps. By comparing the effects of using different architectures, we provide insights into improving automated polyp characterization through histology image analysis.

In the context of zero-error source coding, our investigation focuses on the maximal possible leakage from codewords to source codes, given certain constraints on average Gaspard distance, which measures the guessing power of an adversarial agent attempting to predict the source state from the codeword. We establish a precise upper limit on this entropy leakage by utilizing a specific distance measure known as the $\chi^2$-distance on the code's entropy distribution. We also demonstrate that for specific conditions, this upper limit is indeed the most accurate bound possible. We demonstrate the practical relevance and effectiveness of our findings through numerical experiments on the binary erasure channel model and high-dimensional source models featuring independent components from various distributions.

Deep learning techniques, particularly generative models, have effectively tackled complex problems in various domains, including creating images from limited data points. This paper presents an application of these models to a novel problem: reconstructing a series of related images from a reduced number of compression measurements. A dataset consisting of multiple cat faces was created to assess a model's capacity to link consecutive images of the same subject. The study compared two models, one based on pre-trained statistics and another that was co-trained with data, to determine how well they could identify and recover original images from scarce data points. Notably, the paper highlights the significance of using the same method to collect data as that used to train the model. The results demonstrate the potential for using generative models to efficiently compress high-dimensional data before applying a linear compression technique.

A proposed method involves using the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm to create an approximation of the Ground State of Hamiltonians with sparse and random diagonal entries by optimizing a parameterized circuit with limited depth. To efficiently optimize these parameters, we utilize evolutionary strategies optimized for black-box problems, resulting in substantial reductions in computational requirements compared to conventional observation-based approaches. Our approach demonstrates a significant decrease in the number of required circuit evaluations when applied to the QAOA for combinatorial problems, and experimental results were obtained through simulations of the circuit-based implementation on a superconducting quantum processor, solving instances of the Maximum Clique Problem at a circuit depth feasible for current quantum hardware.

A comprehensive method is presented for determining the area of segments formed by intersecting lines with ellipses, including a derivation of the general equation, demonstration of its correctness through a traditional approach, examination of potential errors, and analysis of its behavior in various cases. Additionally, the formula's efficiency is enhanced through the use of an optimized approximation for square root functions developed by M. Bourbaki.

Building upon the work of Goyal et al. (2021), who introduced a dynamic approach to reinforcement learning, this work extends their q-function for continuous Markov decision processes (MCDPs) over a general state space, which incorporates both a value function and an action-specific indicator function. These functions enable an instantaneous advantage function, which, under certain regularity conditions, leads to an "instantaneous advantage rate" (IAR) function. The IAR function measures how much better or worse a specific control action is compared to another, permitting a value function to be determined as the unique equilibrium of this function. Furthermore, this work presents a dynamic programming equation that has a unique non-negative bounded solution, which, together with an action-specific indicator function, can be shown to satisfy the quantum Hamilton-Jacobi system (QS). The q-function is then utilized to develop reinforcement learning algorithms, which converge to the equilibrium of the quantum Hamilton-Jacobi system, along with an accompanying cost function.

We've discovered a type of magnetic excitation known as magnon, which doesn't require any thermal energy to create, occurring in a specific pattern on a triangular lattice. We've found the conditions for this to happen in the triangular lattice Hubbard model by applying a theory that approximates interactions between electrons by counting their pairings. When applied to this model, it gives a clear result that matches our previous discovery. However, for more complex patterns of magnetism, the application of this theory becomes significantly more complicated. We've used a different approach to analyze the model near the point where these non-thermal excitations occur, which involves evaluating electron interactions. We've found that the model doesn't allow for these non-thermal excitations in most cases of magnetic activity, apart from those that are stable due to the structure of the lattice. We've also examined areas of the lattice that are resistant to these non-thermal excitations, which may be relevant to understanding magnetic properties in materials that are not perfectly ordered.

A crucial aspect of the clinical aorta pipeline, vertebra localization and identification has limited progress due to the lack of high-quality publicly accessible datasets. Real-world medical data often contains imperfections due to data collection limitations and patient conditions, which pose significant challenges for model development. To address these issues, we've developed a comprehensive dataset called CVMI, consisting of various data types from different patient conditions, which we used to evaluate the performance of a range of segmentation-based and compact model architectures. Our analysis reveals that while state-of-the-art models excel at identifying vertebrae, they may struggle with more challenging pathologies and suggest that simple model augmentation can yield comparable results to complex models.

Stochastic thermodynamics uses mathematical models to study how small systems behave over time. This field uses Fokker-Planck equations to describe stochastic trajectories of continuous systems and their associated thermodynamic properties. A systematic approach has been developed to compute key statistical functions, such as the scaled cumulant-generating function, which can be applied across various stochastic processes regardless of specific dynamics. This approach generically extends existing methods and offers alternative analytical solutions within specific cases.

This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. These intersections can be expressed as smooth families over a projective line. Notably, this paper establishes that relative quantum cohomology at specific points along the projective line can be expressed in terms of relative I-functions from other points, including those of different classes. This finding holds the potential to simplify the study of relative I-functions for a more complex class of varieties known as Fano complete intersections.

Two piezoelectric materials placed near each other can transfer energy across an intervening vacuum gap by transmitting acoustic waves. Our research provides a mathematical explanation for how this energy transfer is transmitted, and reveals that specific conditions allow for complete transmission. This finding has the potential to be applied in the design of highly efficient piezoelectric systems used in power and signal transmission applications.

A cutting-edge approach to optically manipulating polariton condensates leverages a two-laser system that interacts with a three-level material. These polariton condensates, formed by the unique properties of light and matter, exhibit unique characteristics when they interact strongly, going beyond typical optical effects. By combining two lasers in a specific configuration, we've discovered a unique way to harness excitons within polaritons, which is essential for their self-interaction. Notably, our method allows for precise control over spatial and temporal variables, which is impossible to achieve with single laser light. As a result, our optical technique offers new possibilities for manipulating light and provides valuable insights into light-matter interactions, ultimately paving the way for new ultra-fast devices.

The disintegrating exoplanet K2-22b displays unique features that require further investigation. Although initial studies have provided some insights into the disintegration process, they lack comprehensive understanding of the surrounding environment. This study presents the first 3D hydrodynamic simulations of this exoplanet and its context, utilizing prior observational data to predict disintegrating dust cloud properties under different scenarios. Notably, simulations align with observed transit spectra, suggesting a low metallic content in the hot, ionized gas present, as well with the size of detected dust particles. Furthermore, calculations based on simulations indicate that dust-driven magnetic fields could generate observable radio waves, a prediction that could be verified through future observations, potentially by the SKA. This research provides a framework for modeling disintegrating exoplanets, enabling predictions for further observational studies.

We develop a novel algebro-geometric approach to studying the Milnor fibration and establish a significant standard for continuous functions, which we use to prove a longstanding hypothesis of Scheiderer. Furthermore, in cases where the hypersurface is defined by the intersection of hyperplanes, we derive a formula that generalizes early work of King.

DaPy is an open-source, teaching-oriented programming language focused on data analysis. Similar to Python, it is also rooted in numerical computation, but DaPy distinguishes itself by incorporating advanced data science capabilities directly into its core design. In contrast to existing data science frameworks, which are add-ons to Python, DaPy integrates these features seamlessly into its native codebase. This project report outlines the implementation of a linear algebra library within DaPy, highlighting its integration of essential data manipulation tools, such as efficient sorting algorithms, customized exception handling, and a user-friendly interface. DaPy's linear algebra library is built using a combination of techniques, including expression templates, dynamic array management, and a decision tree-based approach for operation optimization, all implemented in C++11.

This article revisits the long-standing debate about the origins of scientific experimentation, focusing on the role mathematics played in shaping research methods. By analyzing Galileo's case, the article proposes a new perspective, suggesting that Galileo's non-geometric mathematical skills, specifically arithmetic and geometric proportions, prompted him to integrate theoretical calculations with practical experiments. Ultimately, this contributed to the development of scientific experimentation.

A 2017 study by S. Peimann introduced a useful set of thermodynamic properties that facilitate an in-depth understanding of how equilibrium processes function. Building upon this concept, the researchers expanded its application to analyze complex plasma systems, encompassing various species such as electrons, ions, and neutral atoms in a general equilibrium state. By utilizing the thermodynamic properties, the team successfully derived key formulas for generalized pressure and internal energy in multi-species plasma systems, providing a comprehensive mathematical framework in doing so. Furthermore, the researchers applied these generalized properties to elucidate fundamental processes governing ionization and recombination equilibrium, in addition to examining electron ionization and collisional ionization equilibrium under specific conditions.

In magnetic reconnection research, various scales require different treatment methods, and kinetic approaches are particularly important for studying collisionless phenomena. To overcome the high computational cost of kinetic codes in this field, we adapt an existing hydrodynamic code to include kinetic effects. By using an 8-node, 12-core GPU cluster, we demonstrate the code's capabilities through several magnetic reconnection simulations, including a 2D and 3D island model, and an X-point model in 2D, 2.5, and 3D configurations. Our simulations highlight the importance of accurate initial conditions, and we explore various aspects of the kinetic physics, such as the electron distribution function, and the parallel and perpendicular temperatures of electron and ion distributions. These tests showcase the code's accuracy, and we emphasize the need for precise implementations of key hydrodynamic quantities to obtain reliable results.
